items.html: Auricular laceration. A full-thickness break in the skin and cartilage, it is an open wound rather than a swelling.
cites: Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 43

src.question: Name the condition shown.
src.key: Auricular laceration
src.explanation: A full-thickness break in the skin and cartilage — an open wound rather than a swelling.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Tinnitus, and the masses you can see
items.html: Exostoses. These are multiple smooth bony swellings of the canal wall that narrow the lumen but are covered by normal skin.
cites: Disorders of the Inner Ear, Slide 49

src.question: Name the condition shown.
src.key: Exostoses
src.explanation: Multiple smooth bony swellings of the canal wall, narrowing the lumen but covered by normal skin.

items.html: Salivary tumors and gland size. The smaller the gland, the higher the proportion that are malignant: parotid tumors are 75 to 80 percent benign, submandibular 50 to 60 percent, and minor salivary gland tumors only about 35 percent.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 139

src.question: A 54-year-old has a painless, slowly enlarging 1.5 cm firm swelling of the hard palate, present for eight months. There is no pain, no facial weakness and no cervical lymphadenopathy. A friend whose parotid lump proved benign has told the patient not to worry. What should this patient be told about how the site affects the risk of malignancy?
src.key: The smaller the gland, the higher the proportion that are malignant
src.explanation: Parotid tumors are 75 to 80 percent benign, submandibular 50 to 60 percent, and minor salivary glands only about 35 percent benign. The relationship runs inversely with gland size, which is a memorable rule and changes how aggressively a small-gland lesion is investigated.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Weber, Rinne, and reading the two tracings
items.html: Wax removal with possible drum defect. Irrigation is contraindicated when the drum may not be intact, since water forced into the middle ear causes suppurative otitis media; use microsuction or a curette under direct vision.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 28

src.question: A 60-year-old man needs wax removed. He has a history of a tympanic membrane perforation repaired years ago. What is the most appropriate method of removal?
src.key: Microsuction or curette under direct vision
src.explanation: Irrigation is contraindicated when the drum may not be intact, because water forced into the middle ear seeds it with canal organisms and causes a suppurative otitis media. Removing the wax under direct vision keeps the procedure entirely within the canal and lets the operator see the drum as it is uncovered.

items.html: Cervical node features suggesting malignancy. Immobility (fixation to surrounding structures by tumor) and non-tenderness (inflamed nodes hurt) suggest malignancy. Persistence or continued enlargement triggers fine needle aspiration.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 93

src.question: A 58-year-old smoker is found to have a 3 cm cervical node on a routine visit. It has been present for about six weeks. There has been no fever, sore throat or recent illness, and no weight loss. The clinician is deciding whether this warrants urgent investigation. Which features on palpation would most suggest malignancy?
src.key: Immobility and non-tenderness
src.explanation: The descriptors that matter are: size, shape, mobility, consistency and tenderness. An immobile node suggests fixation to surrounding structures by tumor, and non-tenderness points away from an inflammatory cause, since inflamed nodes hurt. Persistence or continued enlargement is what triggers fine needle aspiration.

items.html: Neck mass by age. Under 40 most neck masses are inflammatory, except Hodgkin lymphoma; above 40 the probability shifts toward malignancy.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 13

src.question: A 27-year-old presents with a firm, painless 2 cm lateral neck mass that has been present for two months. There is no fever, sore throat or recent infection, and no night sweats or weight loss. Examination is otherwise unremarkable. Before any test is ordered, what is the most likely nature of this mass?
src.key: Under 40 most are inflammatory, except Hodgkin lymphoma
src.explanation: Most neck masses in patients under 40 are inflammatory in nature, and names Hodgkin lymphoma as the specific exception to that rule. Above 40 the probability shifts toward malignancy, which is why age over 40 appears on the red-flag list alongside size, duration, firmness and tobacco use.

items.html: Invasive fungal sinusitis. Black necrotic mucosa in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient indicates angioinvasive fungal disease; because the blood supply is destroyed, surgical debridement is needed alongside systemic therapy and control of the diabetes.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 28

src.question: A 63-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has facial pain, black necrotic tissue visible on the nasal turbinate, and rapidly progressive periorbital swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Invasive fungal sinusitis, needing debridement
src.explanation: Black necrotic mucosa in an immunocompromised or diabetic patient indicates angioinvasive fungal disease, where hyphae invade blood vessels and cause tissue infarction. The blood supply is destroyed, so antifungal drugs alone cannot reach the dead tissue; surgical debridement is required alongside systemic therapy and control of the diabetes.

items.html: Adenoidal hypertrophy. Chronic mouth breathing, snoring and hyponasal speech with bilateral nasal obstruction and no discharge indicate it; the bilateral, discharge-free pattern distinguishes it from a foreign body or infection.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 63

src.question: A 5-year-old has chronic mouth breathing, snoring and hyponasal speech with bilateral nasal obstruction. There is no discharge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Adenoidal hypertrophy
src.explanation: The adenoid sits in the nasopharynx behind the nasal cavity, so enlargement obstructs both sides equally and produces mouth breathing, snoring and the hyponasal voice of a blocked nose. The bilateral, discharge-free pattern is what distinguishes it from a foreign body or infection.

items.html: Canal versus middle ear disease. Pain on moving the tragus or pinna localizes disease to the canal, because middle ear infection sits behind an intact drum and is unaffected by moving the external ear.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 40

src.question: A 9-year-old has a 2-day history of left ear pain. The canal is too swollen and tender to admit the speculum, so the drum cannot be seen, and the clinician cannot say whether the problem is in the canal or the middle ear. Temperature is 98.9 degrees Fahrenheit. Which bedside maneuver best separates the two?
src.key: Move the tragus or pinna
src.explanation: Pain on manipulating the pinna or tragus localizes the disease to the canal, because moving those structures moves the inflamed canal skin. Middle ear infection sits behind an intact drum and is unaffected by moving the external ear, so the maneuver separates the two before the otoscope is even used.

items.html: Nasal foreign body in a calm child. The first attempt is a parent-delivered positive pressure blow: the parent seals the child's mouth with their own and blows while the unaffected nostril is occluded. It is atraumatic and needs no instruments.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 51

src.question: A 3-year-old has a bead in the left nostril. The child is calm and the object is visible anteriorly. What is the most appropriate first attempt at removal?
src.key: A parent-delivered positive pressure blow
src.explanation: The parent seals the child's mouth with their own and blows while the unaffected nostril is occluded, so the pressure travels through the posterior choana and pushes the object forward. It is atraumatic, needs no instruments, and avoids the risk of pushing the bead deeper that instrumentation carries in a small child.

items.html: Retained ear canal foreign body. A porous object obstructs drainage and acts as a nidus for infection; foul unilateral discharge without pain or fever in a young child should prompt a search for something in the canal.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 47

src.question: A 5-year-old girl has had a foul-smelling discharge from the left ear for a week. She has been afebrile with no ear pain. Otoscopy after suctioning reveals a small piece of foam rubber impacted against the drum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Retained foreign body with infection
src.explanation: An organic or porous object retained in the canal obstructs drainage and acts as a nidus, so the canal skin becomes secondarily infected and produces the foul discharge. The absence of pain and fever, with a unilateral offensive discharge in a young child, is the pattern that should prompt a careful search for something in the canal.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Tinnitus, and the masses you can see
items.html: Temporary threshold shift. Intense sound temporarily fatigues cochlear hair cells, and hearing recovers within 24 to 48 hours; repeated temporary shifts eventually become permanent, so recovery is a warning rather than a reassurance.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 44

src.question: A 31-year-old man attends a loud concert and afterwards notices muffled hearing and ringing in both ears. By two days later his hearing has returned to normal, though the ringing lingers briefly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: A temporary threshold shift, which recovers within 24 to 48 hours
src.explanation: Intense sound temporarily fatigues the cochlear hair cells, raising the threshold at which sound is detected, and function returns as the cells recover over 24 to 48 hours. The clinical importance is that repeated temporary shifts eventually become permanent, so the recovery is a warning rather than a reassurance.

items.html: Impaired mucociliary clearance. The cilia can no longer move the mucus blanket out of the sinus: chronic inflammation damages the cilia and thickens the mucus, so secretions stagnate and invite repeated infection.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 25

src.question: A 47-year-old man with chronic rhinosinusitis is told the underlying problem is impaired mucociliary clearance. He asks what that means. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: The cilia can no longer move the mucus blanket out of the sinus
src.explanation: Sinus mucosa is lined with ciliated epithelium that sweeps a mucus layer toward the ostium in a fixed direction. Chronic inflammation damages the cilia and thickens the mucus, so secretions stagnate in the sinus, which perpetuates inflammation and invites repeated infection. That is why chronic disease behaves differently from a single acute infection.

items.html: Otosclerosis counseling. It often runs in families and may worsen during pregnancy.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 65

src.question: A 28-year-old woman with otosclerosis asks about the risk to her children. What should the patient be told?
src.key: It often runs in families and may worsen during pregnancy
src.explanation: Otosclerosis has a strong familial tendency, which is why a family history supports the diagnosis. Progression during pregnancy is also recognized, which is relevant counseling for a woman of childbearing age who is deciding when to have surgery.

items.html: Vertigo after ear trauma. A simple perforation does not cause vertigo, so vertigo calls for urgent assessment for inner ear injury (ossicular disruption with perilymphatic fistula, or labyrinthine injury) as well as for a perforation.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 61

src.question: A 21-year-old man is struck on the ear with an open hand and has immediate pain, hearing loss and vertigo, with blood in the canal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Assess urgently for inner ear injury as well as a perforation
src.explanation: Vertigo after ear trauma is the finding that changes the picture. A simple perforation does not cause vertigo, so its presence raises the possibility of ossicular disruption with a perilymphatic fistula or direct labyrinthine injury, which needs prompt specialist assessment rather than routine review.

items.html: Orbital cellulitis from sinusitis. Periorbital swelling with painful restricted eye movement and diplopia means infection has crossed the paper-thin lamina papyracea from the ethmoid sinus; it needs urgent imaging and admission for intravenous antibiotics.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 20

src.question: A 19-year-old man with a week of sinusitis symptoms now has swelling and erythema around the right eye, pain on eye movement and double vision. He is febrile. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Urgent imaging and admission for intravenous antibiotics
src.explanation: Periorbital swelling with painful restricted eye movement and diplopia means the infection has crossed from the sinus into the orbit, because the ethmoid sinus is separated from it only by the paper-thin lamina papyracea. That is orbital cellulitis, which threatens vision and can spread intracranially, so it needs imaging and intravenous therapy now.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Tinnitus, and the masses you can see
items.html: Exostoses (surfer's ear). Repeated exposure to cold water stimulates new bone formation in the canal walls, giving bilateral, symmetrical swellings that trap water and debris and cause recurrent otitis externa.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 49

src.question: A 32-year-old competitive surfer has bilateral, symmetrical, smooth bony swellings narrowing both ear canals. He reports recurrent trapped water and occasional infections. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Exostoses
src.explanation: Repeated exposure to cold water stimulates new bone formation in the canal walls, which is why the condition is known as surfer's ear and why it is bilateral and symmetrical. The clinical consequence is a narrowed canal that traps water and debris, producing the recurrent otitis externa he describes.

items.html: Autoimmune inner ear disease. Rapidly progressive bilateral sensorineural loss is managed with a trial of systemic corticosteroids, which is both therapy and a diagnostic test, as it is one of the few sensorineural losses that responds to treatment.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 64

src.question: A 42-year-old woman with rapidly progressive bilateral sensorineural loss is suspected of having autoimmune inner ear disease. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: A trial of systemic corticosteroids
src.explanation: Autoimmune inner ear disease is one of the few sensorineural losses that responds to treatment, and the response to systemic corticosteroids serves as both therapy and a diagnostic test, since the condition is otherwise hard to confirm. That responsiveness is the reason it must be considered before a bilateral progressive loss is written off.

items.html: Epistaxis on anticoagulation. Clotting studies are not routine in epistaxis but are indicated in anticoagulated patients; correct the anticoagulation as well as treating the nose, or the systemic reason for bleeding is left unaddressed.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 44

src.question: A 78-year-old woman on warfarin has a nosebleed that has stopped with pressure. Her international normalized ratio is 6.2. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Correct the anticoagulation as well as treating the nose
src.explanation: Clotting studies are not routine in epistaxis but are indicated in anticoagulated patients, and this result is well above range. Treating only the local bleeding point leaves the systemic reason it bled and the risk of rebleeding or of hemorrhage elsewhere entirely unaddressed.

items.html: Septal perforation from topical agents. The anterior septum has thin mucosa over cartilage with no other blood supply, so chronic ischemia from prolonged intranasal steroid (especially sprayed at the septum) or cocaine can perforate it.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 29

src.question: A 39-year-old man has nasal crusting, whistling on inspiration and recurrent minor nosebleeds. Examination shows a septal perforation. He has used intranasal steroid for years for allergic rhinitis. What is the most likely cause?
src.key: Chronic ischemia from a topical agent
src.explanation: The anterior septum has a thin mucosa over cartilage with no other blood supply, so anything that causes sustained vasoconstriction or mucosal injury there can perforate it. Prolonged intranasal steroid, particularly if sprayed at the septum rather than laterally, and cocaine are the two named causes, and the history has to ask about both.

items.html: Suspected canal carcinoma. Otitis externa unresponsive to appropriate treatment, with bloody otorrhea and friable tissue, needs biopsy of the canal lesion, since only histology distinguishes malignancy from chronic inflammation.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 71

src.question: A 68-year-old man has had a discharging left ear for four months. It has not responded to three different topical antibiotics. The discharge is now blood-stained and he has developed deep aching pain. Otoscopy shows friable tissue in the canal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Biopsy of the canal lesion
src.explanation: Otitis externa that will not respond to appropriate treatment, together with bloody otorrhea and friable tissue, is the described presentation of canal carcinoma. Only histology distinguishes malignancy from chronic inflammation or granulation, and the treatment pathway is entirely different, so tissue has to be obtained rather than another drop tried.

items.html: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss. It is a syndrome rather than a disease, and a cause is often never found; because the differential includes treatable and dangerous entries, it prompts urgent referral and imaging.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 68

src.question: A 44-year-old man develops unilateral hearing loss over two days with no identifiable cause after investigation. He asks what the diagnosis actually means. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: It is a syndrome rather than a disease, and a cause is often never found
src.explanation: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss describes a pattern of presentation, not a single pathology, and in most cases no cause is identified despite investigation. The clinical importance is that the differential includes treatable and dangerous entries, which is why it prompts urgent referral and imaging rather than a wait to see what happens.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The inner ear syndromes — sorted by how long the vertigo lasts
items.html: Vestibular neuronitis counseling. It is benign and self-limiting and settles over days to weeks; patients should move about rather than lie still, since bed rest and vestibular suppressants delay central compensation.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 93

src.question: A 40-year-old man with vestibular neuronitis asks how long the vertigo will last and what he should do. What should the patient be told?
src.key: It settles over days to weeks; move about rather than lie still
src.explanation: The condition is benign and self-limiting, and recovery depends on central compensation, which is driven by vestibular activity. Prolonged bed rest and continued vestibular suppressants both delay that process, so early mobilization is what shortens the illness.

items.html: Chronic granulomatous sialadenitis. Chronic gland swelling with minimal pain is the picture; consider primary tuberculosis where risk factors exist. The wide differential (cat scratch disease, sarcoidosis, actinomycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, syphilis) means fine needle aspiration biopsy is needed.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 34

src.question: A 68-year-old man has had chronic unilateral parotid swelling with minimal pain for several months. He has risk factors for tuberculosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Chronic granulomatous sialadenitis
src.explanation: Chronic unilateral or bilateral gland swelling with minimal pain is the picture of granulomatous sialadenitis, and primary tuberculosis should be considered when risk factors are present. The differential is wide, including cat scratch disease, sarcoidosis, actinomycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and syphilis, so aspiration biopsy is needed.

also.explanation: Chronic unilateral or bilateral swelling with minimal pain is the picture, and primary tuberculosis should be considered where risk factors exist. The differential is wide, including cat scratch disease, sarcoidosis, actinomycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and syphilis, so fine needle aspiration biopsy is needed.

items.html: Ear discharge character. Scanty discharge suggests the canal, which has no mucous glands; mucoid discharge suggests the middle ear, where mucous membrane exists, and profuse mucoid otorrhea comes through a perforation.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 31

src.question: A 26-year-old has had discharge from the left ear for four days with mild discomfort. The clinician notes the discharge is scanty rather than profuse, and is trying to work out whether the problem lies in the canal or behind the drum, which cannot be seen clearly. How does the character of the discharge help localize it?
src.key: Scanty suggests canal, mucoid suggests middle ear
src.explanation: The canal has no mucous glands, so discharge arising there is scanty, often itchy, and made of desquamated skin and exudate. Mucoid discharge implies mucous membrane, which exists in the middle ear, so profuse mucoid otorrhea indicates it is coming through a perforation rather than from the canal itself.

items.html: Embedded earring back. It should be removed because infection is the main risk; removal treats the source and prevents spread into the auricular cartilage, where perichondritis can deform the ear.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 48

src.question: A 13-year-old girl has an earring back embedded in the soft tissue of the earlobe, with surrounding erythema and tenderness. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Remove it, because infection is the main risk
src.explanation: An embedded earring back is a retained foreign body sitting in soft tissue that has closed over it, and the described erythema and tenderness show infection is already established. Removal is both the treatment of the infection's source and the prevention of spread into the auricular cartilage, where perichondritis can deform the ear.

items.html: Sinusitis with immunosuppression. Management needs earlier imaging and a lower threshold for invasive fungal disease, because Aspergillus and the mucormycetes can invade blood vessels and cause tissue infarction within days; inspect the nasal mucosa for necrotic tissue.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 28

src.question: A 58-year-old woman on chemotherapy has facial pain and fever with sinus opacification. Her clinician notes that the usual approach may need to change. How should her management differ?
src.key: She needs earlier imaging and a lower threshold for invasive fungal disease
src.explanation: Immunosuppression removes the neutrophil response that normally contains fungal hyphae, so Aspergillus and the mucormycetes can invade blood vessels and cause tissue infarction within days. That is why the usual watchful approach to sinusitis is abandoned and why the nasal mucosa is inspected specifically for necrotic tissue.

items.html: Brisk epistaxis with hemodynamic compromise. Dizziness and confusion mean an intravenous line and fluids come first, since resuscitation precedes control of the bleeding point. Bilateral bleeding with no visible source suggests a posterior (sphenopalatine artery) bleed.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 40

src.question: A 73-year-old man comes to the emergency department with a nosebleed lasting over two hours. There is no trauma and no bleeding disorder. He is holding a blood-soaked towel; there is brisk bleeding from both nostrils and the site cannot be seen. He feels dizzy and appears confused. What should be done first?
src.key: Start an intravenous line and give fluids
src.explanation: Dizziness and confusion in someone who has bled briskly for two hours are signs of hemodynamic compromise, and resuscitation precedes definitive control of the bleeding point. Bleeding from both nostrils with no visible anterior source suggests a posterior bleed from the sphenopalatine artery, which is the type that causes significant blood loss.

items.html: Epistaxis first aid. Pinch the soft part (alae) continuously for ten minutes, leaning forward. The bleeding point in 90 percent of cases is Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior septum; leaning forward stops blood tracking into the pharynx.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 41

src.question: A 19-year-old has a nosebleed that started spontaneously twenty minutes ago and is still bleeding. There is no trauma, no anticoagulant use and no bleeding history. The bleeding appears to be coming from the front of the septum. What first aid instruction should be given?
src.key: Pinch the soft part for ten minutes, leaning forward
src.explanation: The bleeding point in 90 percent of cases is Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior septum, which is compressed by pinching the alae rather than the bony bridge. Continuous pressure matters because releasing to check disrupts the forming clot, and leaning forward stops blood tracking backward into the pharynx where it is swallowed or aspirated.

items.html: Diving barotrauma. Persistent vertigo and sensorineural loss after diving suggest inner ear barotrauma with possible perilymphatic fistula, from a ruptured round or oval window membrane; it needs prompt specialist assessment and avoidance of straining.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 37

src.question: A 32-year-old diver has ear pain and vertigo on ascent, with hearing loss that has not settled after several hours. What should be suspected?
src.key: Suspect inner ear barotrauma with a possible perilymphatic fistula
src.explanation: Middle ear barotrauma alone causes pain and conductive loss that settle as the effusion clears. Persistent vertigo and sensorineural loss after diving suggest the pressure change has ruptured a round or oval window membrane, letting perilymph leak, which needs prompt specialist assessment and avoidance of straining.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The inner ear syndromes — sorted by how long the vertigo lasts
items.html: Otosyphilis. Syphilis can mimic Meniere disease exactly and is worth excluding serologically, because it has a specific curative treatment while Meniere does not.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 66

src.question: A 46-year-old man has fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss with episodic vertigo and tinnitus, clinically indistinguishable from Meniere disease. His clinician orders serologic testing before settling on the diagnosis. What is being looked for, and why?
src.key: Syphilis, which mimics Meniere
src.explanation: Otosyphilis can reproduce the Meniere picture exactly, and the reason it is worth excluding is that it has a specific curative treatment while Meniere does not. Missing it means committing a patient to symptomatic management of an incurable syndrome when the underlying infection could have been eradicated.

items.html: Epistaxis with clots. Blow out clots first, since retained clot holds the vessel open; then spray a topical vasoconstrictor such as oxymetazoline and pinch the alae continuously for ten minutes.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 41

src.question: A 47-year-old is having a nosebleed and there are visible clots in both nostrils. The patient has been holding a tissue to the nose for ten minutes without pressure and asks whether it is safe to blow the nose before pinching it. What should the patient be told?
src.key: Blow out clots first, then apply pressure and a vasoconstrictor
src.explanation: Retained clot holds the vessel open and prevents the mucosal edges from apposing, so clearing it lets a fresh clot form against a compressed vessel. The sequence is to blow out clots, spray a topical vasoconstrictor such as oxymetazoline, then pinch the alae continuously for ten minutes.

items.html: Vasomotor rhinitis. Clear bilateral rhinorrhea triggered by cold air, strong smells and alcohol, with no itch and negative allergy testing, is driven by autonomic dysregulation rather than an immunoglobulin E response.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 66

src.question: A 48-year-old man has clear bilateral rhinorrhea triggered by cold air, strong smells and alcohol. He has no itch, no sneezing paroxysms and negative allergy testing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Vasomotor rhinitis
src.explanation: Vasomotor rhinitis produces clear bilateral discharge like allergic rhinitis, which is why they are considered together, but it is driven by autonomic dysregulation rather than an immunoglobulin E response. The triggers are physical and chemical rather than allergenic, and itch and ocular symptoms are characteristically absent.

items.html: Allergic rhinitis and the ear. Mucosal edema obstructs the eustachian tube, which is lined by the same respiratory mucosa as the nose; trapped middle ear air is absorbed, the drum retracts, and fullness with popping results.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 22

src.question: A 41-year-old man with allergic rhinitis has recurrent ear fullness and popping. A student asks why allergy affects the ear. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: Mucosal edema obstructs the eustachian tube
src.explanation: The eustachian tube is lined by the same respiratory mucosa as the nose, so allergic inflammation swells it and closes the lumen. Once the tube cannot open, the trapped middle ear air is absorbed, pressure falls below atmospheric, the drum retracts and the patient feels fullness with popping as the tube intermittently opens.

items.html: Sinusitis pain on bending. Bending forward increases the hydrostatic pressure of the fluid within the obstructed sinus against inflamed mucosa; postural worsening is characteristic of sinusitis.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 12

src.question: A 29-year-old woman with sinusitis asks why her face hurts more when she leans forward to tie her shoes. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: Bending increases the hydrostatic pressure of the fluid within the sinus
src.explanation: An obstructed sinus fills with fluid under pressure, and tilting the head forward raises the column of fluid pressing against the inflamed mucosa and its sensory nerve endings. That is why postural worsening is such a characteristic feature of sinusitis and helps separate it from other causes of facial pain.

items.html: Imaging in sudden hearing loss. Magnetic resonance imaging is done to exclude a retrocochlear lesion such as a schwannoma, because a proportion of sudden loss turns out to be vestibular schwannoma and clinical features cannot identify them.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 68

src.question: A 45-year-old developed hearing loss in the right ear over 48 hours, noticed on waking. There is no pain, discharge, trauma or noise exposure. Otoscopy is normal, the Weber lateralizes to the left and the Rinne is air greater than bone bilaterally. Steroids are started and magnetic resonance imaging is ordered. What is the reason for the imaging?
src.key: To exclude a retrocochlear lesion such as a schwannoma
src.explanation: A proportion of patients presenting with sudden loss turn out to have a vestibular schwannoma, and the presentation gives no reliable way to identify them clinically. Because a tumor's size at diagnosis determines the treatment options and the chance of preserving hearing and facial nerve function, imaging is done rather than assumed unnecessary.

items.html: Flying with a cold. Use a topical decongestant before descent and swallow or yawn frequently; the decongestant shrinks the mucosa around the eustachian tube opening so it can open and equalize pressure.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 37

src.question: A 34-year-old woman with a heavy cold is due to fly and asks how to reduce the risk of ear pain. What advice should the patient be given?
src.key: Use a topical decongestant before descent and swallow or yawn frequently
src.explanation: The problem is a eustachian tube too swollen to equalize the rising ambient pressure during descent. A topical decongestant shrinks the mucosa around the tube opening so it can open, and swallowing, yawning or the Valsalva maneuver actively opens it, letting middle ear pressure track the cabin.

items.html: Suspected perilymphatic fistula. Initial management is bed rest with head elevation and avoidance of straining, since the leak is pressure-dependent; many fistulae close spontaneously before surgical repair is considered.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 60

src.question: A 31-year-old developed hearing loss and vertigo immediately after a heavy weightlifting session, with a sensation of a pop in the right ear. Symptoms worsen on straining and coughing. Otoscopy is normal and a perilymphatic fistula is suspected. What is the most appropriate initial management?
src.key: Bed rest with head elevation and avoidance of straining
src.explanation: The leak is pressure-dependent, which is why symptoms worsen with coughing, lifting and straining. Reducing the pressure gradient by resting with the head up gives the ruptured window membrane a chance to seal, and many fistulae close spontaneously with that alone before surgical repair is considered.

items.html: Childhood anterior epistaxis. Ninety percent of nosebleeds are anterior, from Kiesselbach plexus; digital trauma is the commonest cause and dry winter air worsens it. Short bleeds stopped by pressure in a well child are managed conservatively with humidification and behavior change.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 37

src.question: A 9-year-old boy has recurrent nosebleeds from the left nostril, each stopping within ten minutes with pressure. He has no bruising elsewhere, takes no medication, and picks his nose frequently. It is winter. What is the most likely diagnosis, and how should it be managed?
src.key: Anterior epistaxis, managed conservatively
src.explanation: Ninety percent of nosebleeds are anterior, arising from Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior septum where several arteries anastomose in thin mucosa. Digital trauma is the commonest cause, and dry winter air cracks the mucosa further. Short bleeds stopped by pressure in a well child need humidification and behavior change rather than investigation.

items.html: Ototoxic drug classes. Aminoglycosides destroy cochlear hair cells, usually permanently, starting at high frequencies; loop diuretics affect the stria vascularis and their effect is more often reversible.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 32

src.question: A 68-year-old being treated for a severe Gram-negative infection develops tinnitus and reduced hearing after twelve days of intravenous therapy. Renal function has also declined. The clinician reviews the medication list for the classes most associated with cochlear toxicity. Which drug classes are most likely responsible?
src.key: Aminoglycosides and loop diuretics
src.explanation: Aminoglycosides accumulate in and destroy cochlear hair cells, usually permanently, starting at the high frequencies. Loop diuretics affect the stria vascularis and their effect is more often reversible. Both appear as named ototoxic classes, and the difference in reversibility matters for what the patient is told.

items.html: Conductive anosmia. Polyps, chronic inflammation or marked mucosal swelling block airflow to the olfactory epithelium, so receptors are intact but never reached; treating the obstruction can restore smell.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 63

src.question: A 55-year-old man has lost his sense of smell over several months, with nasal obstruction and thick discharge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Conductive anosmia from obstruction
src.explanation: Smell requires airflow to carry odorant molecules up to the olfactory epithelium high in the nasal vault. Polyps, chronic inflammation or marked mucosal swelling block that path, so the receptors are intact but never reached. That is why treating the obstruction can restore smell, unlike a sensorineural olfactory loss.

items.html: Central versus peripheral vertigo. Headache, ataxia, or focal neurological signs raise concern for a central cause. Severe truncal ataxia, direction-changing nystagmus, diplopia, dysarthria or facial numbness point to the brainstem or cerebellum and require urgent imaging.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 97

src.question: A 72-year-old with hypertension and atrial fibrillation has had constant vertigo for six hours with vomiting. The clinician must decide between a peripheral and a central cause before the patient is discharged. Which features would raise concern for a central cause?
src.key: Headache, ataxia, or focal neurological signs
src.explanation: Peripheral vertigo produces unidirectional nystagmus and unsteadiness that still allows the patient to sit and walk with support. Severe truncal ataxia, headache, direction-changing nystagmus or any focal deficit such as diplopia, dysarthria or facial numbness point to the brainstem or cerebellum and require urgent imaging.

items.html: Pulsatile neck mass. Pulsatility or a bruit means a vascular lesion, most likely a paraganglioma, which arises at the carotid body, the vagus or the jugulotympanic region. It must not be biopsied blindly and needs computed tomography angiography first.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 13

src.question: A 47-year-old woman has a neck mass that is pulsatile and has an audible bruit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: A vascular lesion, most likely a paraganglioma
src.explanation: There are four rules of thumb, and pulsatility or a bruit means vascular. Paragangliomas head the benign vascular list, arising at the carotid body, the vagus or the jugulotympanic region. The practical consequence is that this mass must not be biopsied blindly and needs computed tomography angiography before anything is put into it.

items.html: Allergic rhinitis treatment. About 80 percent of patients need two or more agents because different symptoms are driven by different mediators. A typical combination is an antihistamine with an intranasal corticosteroid, adding a leukotriene inhibitor at night, and immunotherapy if drugs are insufficient.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 67

src.question: A 26-year-old man with perennial allergic rhinitis has persistent symptoms on a single antihistamine. He asks what usually happens next. What should the patient be told?
src.key: Most patients end up on more than one medicine
src.explanation: About 80 percent of patients with allergic rhinitis require two or more agents, because the different symptoms are driven by different mediators. A typical combination is an antihistamine with an intranasal corticosteroid, adding a leukotriene inhibitor at night, and immunotherapy if drug treatment is insufficient.

items.html: Squamous cell neck node. The neck disease is a metastasis, so the primary must be located; its site determines the extent of resection and the radiotherapy field. Every mucosal surface, the thyroid, the salivary glands and the skin are examined systematically.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 39

src.question: A 66-year-old smoker has a firm 4 cm level II neck node. Fine needle aspiration shows squamous cell carcinoma. Examination of the mouth and throat shows no obvious lesion, and the team arranges panendoscopy with directed biopsies before any treatment. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: Treatment fields and surgery both depend on where it came from
src.explanation: The neck disease is a metastasis, so treating it alone leaves the source in place to keep seeding. Locating the primary determines the extent of resection and the radiotherapy field, which is why a systematic examination is made of every mucosal surface, the thyroid, the salivary glands and the skin.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Tinnitus, and the masses you can see
items.html: Jugular foramen mass. A tumor at the jugular foramen compresses cranial nerves nine, ten and eleven (glossopharyngeal, vagus, spinal accessory), causing difficulty swallowing, hoarseness and shoulder weakness alongside pulsatile tinnitus and conductive loss.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 51

src.question: A 57-year-old has pulsatile tinnitus and progressive hearing loss on the left. On examination there is hoarseness, a weak shoulder shrug and the tongue deviates on protrusion. Imaging shows a vascular mass at the jugular foramen. Which cranial nerves does this lesion involve?
src.key: Cranial nerves nine, ten and eleven
src.explanation: The glossopharyngeal, vagus and spinal accessory nerves all pass through the jugular foramen, so a tumor arising there compresses them together. That produces difficulty swallowing, hoarseness and shoulder weakness alongside the pulsatile tinnitus and conductive loss from the middle ear component.

items.html: Bacterial rhinosinusitis. Symptoms persisting ten days or more without improvement help identify the small bacterial minority of rhinosinusitis (90 to 98 percent is viral). Amoxicillin-clavulanate twice daily is first line, as clavulanate covers beta-lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis plus pneumococcus.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 15

src.question: A 25-year-old patient has had ten days of nasal congestion, purulent discharge, facial pressure and reduced sense of smell. Symptoms have not improved with a week of oral decongestants and saline irrigation. Temperature is 100.8 degrees Fahrenheit. There is maxillary sinus tenderness and thick yellow-green discharge. What is the most appropriate treatment?
src.key: Amoxicillin-clavulanate twice daily
src.explanation: Symptoms persisting ten days or more without improvement is one of the criteria that shifts a rhinosinusitis from the 90 to 98 percent that are viral into the small bacterial minority. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is first line because the clavulanate covers the beta-lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis alongside pneumococcus.

items.html: Otitis externa with a swollen canal. When edema stops drops at the outer canal, place an ear wick. It is an absorbent strip that draws medication along the canal by capillary action, restoring delivery without changing the drug.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 41

src.question: A 55-year-old man has had otitis externa treated with drops for five days. The canal is so edematous that the drops appear not to be reaching beyond the outer third, and his pain is unchanged. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Place an ear wick to carry the drops in
src.explanation: Topical therapy only works where the drug physically reaches, and a canal swollen shut stops the drops at its outer end. A wick is an absorbent strip that draws medication along the length of the canal by capillary action, restoring delivery to the inflamed skin without changing the drug.

items.html: Sudden pain relief in otitis media. In acute otitis media pain comes from pus under pressure stretching the drum. When the drum perforates, the pressure is released, pain stops abruptly and discharge appears.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 61

src.question: A 33-year-old woman had severe right ear pain for two days with fever. This morning the pain stopped abruptly and she noticed discharge on her pillow. Otoscopy shows purulent material in the canal and a small perforation in the tympanic membrane. What best explains the sudden change?
src.key: The drum has perforated, releasing the pressure of the middle ear pus
src.explanation: In acute otitis media the pain comes from pus under pressure stretching the drum. Once the drum ruptures the pressure is relieved and the pain stops abruptly, which is why sudden relief accompanied by discharge is the classic history. The perforation is a consequence of the infection, not a separate injury.

items.html: Epistaxis blood tests. Clotting studies (prothrombin time and international normalized ratio) are not routine for epistaxis. They are reserved for anticoagulated patients or those with other evidence of a bleeding tendency.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 44

src.question: A 55-year-old man on no medication has a single anterior nosebleed that stops with pressure. He asks whether he needs blood tests. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: No clotting studies, because they are not routine for epistaxis
src.explanation: Prothrombin time and international normalized ratio are not part of the routine workup and are reserved for patients who are anticoagulated or who have other evidence of a bleeding tendency. Ordering them reflexively generates incidental abnormalities without changing the management of a nosebleed that has already stopped.

items.html: Straightening the canal in a toddler. The infant and toddler canal runs upward from the drum, so pull the pinna downward and backward. In older children and adults the pinna is pulled up and back.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 8

src.question: A clinician is examining the ear of a 2-year-old and needs to straighten the canal. How should the canal be straightened?
src.key: Pull the pinna downward and backward
src.explanation: The infant and toddler canal runs upward from the drum, so the pinna is pulled down and back to align it. In older children and adults the canal takes the opposite course and the pinna is pulled up and back. Using the adult maneuver in a toddler leaves the drum obscured.

items.html: Minor nasal trauma. When tenderness is confined to the bony bridge, each nostril is patent, the nose is straight without septal deviation, and there is no septal hematoma, use ice and elevation without radiography. Treatment of an undisplaced fracture is symptomatic.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 46

src.question: A 27-year-old man is punched in the nose. He has tenderness and swelling isolated to the bony bridge, breathes freely through each nostril, the nose is straight with no septal deviation, and there is no septal hematoma. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Ice and elevation, without radiography
src.explanation: All four reassuring criteria are met: tenderness confined to the bony bridge, patent airflow through each side, a straight nose with no septal deviation, and no septal hematoma. A radiograph would not change management in that situation, because the treatment of an undisplaced nasal fracture is symptomatic in any case.

items.html: Unilateral foul nasal discharge in a child. Unilateral, foul-smelling purulent discharge in a young child is a retained nasal foreign body until proven otherwise. Direct visualization of the nasal vestibule makes the diagnosis and allows removal.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 51

src.question: A 4-year-old boy has had two weeks of purulent nasal discharge. He has been afebrile with no respiratory symptoms. His mother says he gets into everything. Examination shows right-sided purulent discharge that is greenish-brown and extraordinarily foul-smelling. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Direct visualization of the right nasal vestibule
src.explanation: Unilateral, foul-smelling purulent discharge in a young child is a retained nasal foreign body until proven otherwise, because an obstructing object traps secretions that stagnate and become malodorous. Looking directly into the vestibule both makes the diagnosis and allows the object to be removed, which is the treatment.

items.html: Childhood hearing loss urgency. Language acquisition depends on hearing during a limited early-childhood window. Reduced auditory input then produces delays that persist even after hearing is restored, so the threshold to intervene is lower than in adults.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 30

src.question: A 2-year-old has had recurrent middle ear effusions for a year and hearing has been reduced throughout. The child has fewer words than expected for age but is normal in every other respect. The parent asks why this is being treated more urgently than the same problem would be in an adult. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: Language acquisition depends on hearing during a limited window
src.explanation: Speech and language develop during a critical period in early childhood, and reduced auditory input during that window produces delays that persist even after hearing is restored. An adult with the same conductive loss is inconvenienced; a toddler may lose ground that is harder to recover, which is why the threshold to intervene is lower.

items.html: Imaging a suspected thyroid cancer. Use ultrasound, which characterizes nodules without radiation and guides aspiration. Avoid iodine-containing contrast computed tomography, because the iodine load saturates the thyroid and compromises subsequent radioiodine treatment.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 18

src.question: A 49-year-old woman has a firm thyroid nodule with a hoarse voice. The clinician is deciding which imaging to request, and cancer is suspected. Which imaging is most appropriate?
src.key: Ultrasound, avoiding iodine-containing contrast
src.explanation: Ultrasound characterizes thyroid nodules well without radiation and guides aspiration. The specific trap is contrast computed tomography: an iodine load saturates the thyroid and compromises subsequent radioiodine treatment, so it is avoided whenever thyroid cancer is on the differential.

items.html: Aminoglycoside monitoring. Baseline and serial audiometry are used because aminoglycosides damage the outer hair cells at the cochlear base, which encode the highest frequencies. Early detection allows the drug to be changed, as the damage is usually permanent.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 32

src.question: A 59-year-old is starting a six-week course of intravenous gentamicin for endocarditis. Hearing and balance are currently normal. The clinician enrolls the patient in monitoring for cochlear toxicity for the duration of treatment. What should the program involve?
src.key: Baseline and serial audiometry
src.explanation: Aminoglycosides damage the outer hair cells at the cochlear base, which encode the highest frequencies, so loss appears there before it reaches the speech range. Detecting it early allows the drug to be changed before the patient notices any functional problem, which matters because the damage is usually permanent.

items.html: Surgery for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Almost all thyroid cancers require thyroidectomy. The exception is disease localized to one lobe, well differentiated and without metastasis, where lobectomy may be sufficient, preserving the contralateral gland and reducing risk to the recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroids.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 44

src.question: A 29-year-old woman has papillary thyroid carcinoma confined to one lobe, well differentiated, with no evidence of metastasis. What is the appropriate extent of surgery?
src.key: Lobectomy may be sufficient rather than total thyroidectomy
src.explanation: Almost all thyroid cancers require thyroidectomy, with one explicit exception: disease localized to one lobe, well differentiated and without metastasis. That is exactly this patient, and lobectomy preserves the contralateral gland and reduces the risk to the recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroids.

items.html: Nasal trauma imaging. Imaging can be omitted only when all four reassuring criteria are met. A deviated nose or a blocked nostril fails them, so radiography is indicated and the nose is assessed for reduction.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 46

src.question: A 24-year-old woman is struck in the nose. She has swelling, an obviously deviated nose, and cannot breathe through the left nostril. What is the most appropriate imaging?
src.key: Radiography is indicated, because she fails the clinical criteria
src.explanation: Imaging can be omitted only when all four reassuring criteria are met: tenderness confined to the bony bridge, patent airflow through each nostril, a straight nose with no septal deviation, and no septal hematoma. She fails two of them, so the criteria no longer permit a clinical-only approach and the nose has to be imaged and assessed for reduction.

items.html: Button battery in the nose. Urgent removal is required. The battery generates current across moist mucosa, producing hydroxide ions and liquefactive necrosis that can perforate the septum within hours, making it the one nasal foreign body treated as a true emergency.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 51

src.question: A 3-year-old inserted a small button battery into the nose two hours ago. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Urgent removal, because a battery causes rapid liquefactive necrosis
src.explanation: A button battery generates an electrical current across moist mucosa, producing hydroxide ions and liquefactive necrosis that can perforate the septum within hours. That makes it the one nasal foreign body treated as a true emergency, unlike inert beads or foam where the damage is obstruction and secondary infection over days.

items.html: Ethmoid sinusitis and the orbit. The lamina papyracea, the medial orbital wall separating ethmoid from orbit, is paper-thin, the thinnest bone in the orbit. Ethmoid sinusitis is therefore the commonest sinus source of orbital cellulitis, particularly in children.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 6

src.question: A 7-year-old with four days of purulent rhinorrhea develops swelling and redness of the right eyelids, pain on eye movement and mild proptosis. Computed tomography shows opacification of the ethmoid sinuses with a subperiosteal collection in the orbit. Why does the ethmoid sinus in particular threaten the eye?
src.key: The lamina papyracea separating them is paper-thin
src.explanation: The medial orbital wall is formed by the lamina papyracea, literally the papery layer, and it is the thinnest bone in the orbit. Infection in the ethmoid air cells has only that barrier to cross, which is why ethmoid sinusitis is the commonest sinus source of orbital cellulitis, particularly in children.

items.html: Painless discharge in chronic suppurative otitis media. The perforation gives the middle ear a permanent outlet, so pressure never builds and infection appears as discharge rather than pain. Painlessness is the hallmark separating chronic from acute disease.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 31

src.question: A 30-year-old woman with chronic suppurative otitis media asks why her ear discharges but does not hurt. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: The perforation lets the middle ear drain, so pressure never builds
src.explanation: Pain in acute otitis media comes from pus stretching an intact drum. With an established perforation the middle ear has a permanent outlet, so pressure cannot accumulate and the infection expresses itself as discharge rather than pain. That painlessness is the clinical hallmark separating chronic from acute disease.

items.html: Removing a smooth round object from the canal. Forceps push it deeper. Instead, pass a hook or curette beyond it under direct vision and draw it outward, since the risk is pushing the object against or through the drum.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 47

src.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought in after putting a small plastic bead in his right ear canal. He is cooperative, the bead is smooth, round and visible in the outer third of the canal, and the tympanic membrane beyond it appears intact. What is the most appropriate method of removal?
src.key: Removal under direct vision with an instrument passed beyond the object
src.explanation: A smooth round object cannot be grasped by forceps because they simply push it deeper, so the technique is to pass a hook or curette past it under direct vision and draw it outward. Direct visualization matters because the risk of the procedure is pushing the object against or through the drum.

items.html: Septal deviation. An asymptomatic deviation needs no treatment. It is treated only when it causes obstruction, recurrent epistaxis from the drier open side, obstructive sleep apnea, snoring or facial pain.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 30

src.question: A 33-year-old woman has a mildly deviated septum found incidentally. She has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: No treatment, as an asymptomatic deviation needs none
src.explanation: Septal deviation is extremely common and is only treated when it causes symptoms: obstruction, recurrent epistaxis from the drier open side, obstructive sleep apnea, snoring or facial pain. Operating on an incidental finding in an asymptomatic patient offers only the risks of surgery.

items.html: Eustachian tube dysfunction. When the tube cannot ventilate the middle ear, trapped air is absorbed, pressure falls below atmospheric and the drum retracts. Tympanometry shows a type C tympanogram, with the peak shifted to negative pressure.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 22

src.question: A 29-year-old woman has had a blocked, full sensation in both ears since a head cold two weeks ago, with mild hearing reduction and a popping sensation on swallowing. Otoscopy shows retracted tympanic membranes. Tympanometry is performed. Which tympanometry result would be expected?
src.key: A type C tympanogram, with the peak shifted to negative pressure
src.explanation: A eustachian tube that cannot ventilate the middle ear allows the trapped air to be absorbed, so middle ear pressure falls below atmospheric and the drum retracts. Tympanometry measures compliance across a pressure sweep, and the peak compliance shifts to wherever middle ear pressure actually is: negative, which is the definition of a type C trace.

items.html: Sinusitis in children. The same criteria apply as in adults, so ten days of purulent discharge without improvement indicates bacterial sinusitis. Children have maxillary and ethmoid sinuses from birth, and ethmoid proximity to the orbit makes recognition important.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 15

src.question: A 5-year-old has ten days of purulent nasal discharge and cough that has not improved. He is afebrile and otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Bacterial sinusitis, meeting the ten-day criterion
src.explanation: The same criteria apply in children as in adults, and persistence beyond ten days without improvement is one of them. Children have maxillary and ethmoid sinuses from birth, so sinusitis is possible at this age, and the ethmoid proximity to the orbit is what makes recognition important.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Tinnitus, and the masses you can see
items.html: Bilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus. With symmetrical sensorineural loss it is generated centrally as the brain compensates for reduced input. Management is reassurance, hearing aids and sound therapy; amplification often reduces it, and sound therapy reduces the contrast between tinnitus and silence.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 41

src.question: A 63-year-old man has bilateral high-pitched ringing in both ears, present for two years, alongside a symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural loss. There is no pulsatility and no vertigo. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Reassurance, hearing aids and sound therapy
src.explanation: Bilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus accompanying a symmetrical sensorineural loss is the common form, generated centrally as the brain compensates for reduced input. Because the driver is the hearing loss, amplification often reduces the tinnitus, and sound therapy works by reducing the contrast between the tinnitus and silence.

items.html: Nasal injury check. Before discharge, inspect and feel the septum for a boggy swelling. A septal hematoma is easy to miss because attention goes to the bridge, yet it destroys cartilage within days if not drained.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 32

src.question: A 22-year-old was struck on the nose playing football two hours ago. The nose is mildly swollen but appears straight, there is no epistaxis now, and the patient feels the injury is trivial. What should be looked for before the patient is discharged?
src.key: Inspect the septum for a boggy swelling
src.explanation: A septal hematoma is easy to miss because attention goes to the bridge and to whether the nose looks straight, yet it is the one finding that destroys cartilage within days if not drained. Looking specifically at the septum, and feeling it, is what the four-criteria rule makes explicit.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The inner ear syndromes — sorted by how long the vertigo lasts
items.html: Meniere disease self-care. Restricting dietary salt, caffeine and alcohol is advised. The underlying abnormality is endolymphatic hydrops; less sodium lowers fluid retention and endolymph volume, and caffeine and alcohol are recognized triggers.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 80

src.question: A 47-year-old woman with confirmed Meniere disease asks what she can do herself to reduce the frequency of her attacks. What advice should be given?
src.key: Restrict dietary salt, caffeine and alcohol
src.explanation: The underlying abnormality is endolymphatic hydrops, an excess of endolymph distending the membranous labyrinth. Reducing sodium load lowers fluid retention and therefore endolymph volume, and caffeine and alcohol are recognized triggers. These are the measures a patient can act on before any drug is added.

items.html: Clear rhinorrhea after trauma. Clear nasal fluid after significant facial or head trauma, especially with bilateral periorbital bruising, suggests a cerebrospinal fluid leak from a skull base fracture through the cribriform plate. It is a neurosurgical problem with a risk of meningitis.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 46

src.question: A 30-year-old man is assaulted and has clear fluid dripping from one nostril. He also has periorbital bruising on both sides. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Suspect a cerebrospinal fluid leak from a skull base fracture
src.explanation: Clear rhinorrhea after significant facial or head trauma, particularly with bilateral periorbital bruising, raises the possibility that the cribriform plate has fractured and cerebrospinal fluid is draining through the nose. That converts a nasal injury into a neurosurgical problem and carries a risk of meningitis.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The inner ear syndromes — sorted by how long the vertigo lasts
items.html: Meniere disease. It is defined by episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, all in the same ear. Loss is low-frequency because the cochlear apex, which codes low frequencies, distends most from endolymphatic hydrops.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 76

src.question: A 45-year-old man has had four episodes over three months of spinning vertigo lasting two to three hours, each preceded by a sense of fullness and roaring tinnitus in the left ear. His hearing fluctuates and an audiogram during an attack shows low-frequency sensorineural loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Meniere disease
src.explanation: The defining tetrad is episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, all in the same ear. Endolymphatic hydrops distends the membranous labyrinth, and the low-frequency pattern of loss is characteristic because the apex of the cochlea, which codes low frequencies, distends most.

items.html: Swimmer's otitis externa. Treatment must cover Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus. Water raises canal pH and macerates skin, favoring Pseudomonas; topical fluoroquinolones cover both, whereas oral amoxicillin would be inadequate.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 41

src.question: An 11-year-old who swims daily has a 3-day history of right ear pain, itch and scanty discharge. The canal is erythematous and edematous and the pinna is tender to move. Topical treatment is being selected. Which organisms must the treatment cover?
src.key: Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus
src.explanation: Water exposure raises the canal pH and macerates the skin, which favors Pseudomonas in particular, alongside Staphylococcus from the skin flora. Topical fluoroquinolones are chosen because they cover both, and that Pseudomonas coverage is why an oral antibiotic like amoxicillin would be inadequate.

items.html: Acute bacterial parotitis. Dehydration causes salivary stasis, letting bacteria ascend the duct; Staphylococcus aureus is commonest, and pus from Stensen duct confirms infection. Treat with rehydration and antistaphylococcal antibiotics, plus warm compresses, massage and sialogogues.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 38

src.question: A 79-year-old woman is four days after hip surgery and has poor oral intake. She develops unilateral painful swelling over the angle of the jaw with overlying erythema. Pus can be expressed from the duct opposite the upper second molar. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Rehydration and antistaphylococcal antibiotics
src.explanation: Dehydration and reduced oral intake cause salivary stasis, and stasis lets bacteria ascend the parotid duct. Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism, and pus expressible from Stensen duct confirms the gland is infected. Treatment is rehydration, which restores flow, together with penicillinase-resistant gram-positive cover.

also.explanation: Dehydration causes salivary stasis, which lets bacteria ascend the parotid duct. Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism, and pus expressible from Stensen duct confirms the gland is infected. Treatment is rehydration to restore flow plus penicillinase-resistant gram-positive cover, with warm compresses, massage and sialogogues.

items.html: Glottic tumor. Hoarseness is the expected and usually earliest symptom, since a mass replacing the true vocal cord prevents normal vibration and apposition. Referred ear pain reflects shared vagal innervation between the larynx and the ear.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 144

src.question: A 68-year-old with a 50 pack-year smoking history has four months of worsening dysphagia, occasional blood-streaked sputum and intermittent right ear pain on swallowing. Stridor is audible over the trachea. Nasopharyngoscopy shows a mass replacing the right true vocal cord. Which symptom would be expected?
src.key: Hoarseness
src.explanation: A mass replacing the true vocal cord prevents that cord vibrating and apposing normally, and voice production depends on both cords meeting and vibrating together. Hoarseness is therefore the expected and usually earliest symptom of a glottic tumor, and the referred ear pain reflects shared vagal innervation between the larynx and the ear.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Weber, Rinne, and reading the two tracings
items.html: Mixed hearing loss. An air-bone gap indicates a conductive component, and elevated bone conduction thresholds indicate a sensorineural component. Both together define a mixed loss, so correcting the conductive part will not restore normal hearing.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 19

src.question: A 58-year-old has reduced hearing in the left ear. Audiometry shows elevated bone conduction thresholds on the left together with an air-bone gap on the same side. There is a history of both chronic ear infections and long-standing noise exposure at work. What does this pattern indicate?
src.key: A mixed hearing loss
src.explanation: An air-bone gap means sound is being obstructed before it reaches the cochlea, which is conductive. Elevated bone conduction means the cochlea itself is not performing normally, which is sensorineural. Having both together defines a mixed loss, and it matters because correcting the conductive component will not restore hearing to normal.

items.html: Nodal level in neck metastasis. The involved nodal level predicts where the primary is likely to be, because each region drains to a predictable group: jugulodigastric to the tonsil, juguloomohyoid to the tongue, submandibular to the face, sinuses and mouth.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 10

src.question: A 62-year-old smoker has a firm 3 cm node in the posterior triangle. Aspiration confirms squamous cell carcinoma and no primary is visible in the mouth or throat. The team notes which nodal level is involved before planning the search. Why does the level matter?
src.key: The level predicts where the primary is likely to be
src.explanation: Each region of the head and neck drains to a predictable nodal group, so the level of the involved node narrows the search for the primary. That is the practical application of the drainage map: jugulodigastric nodes point to the tonsil, juguloomohyoid to the tongue, and submandibular nodes to the face, sinuses and mouth.

items.html: Suspected non-organic hearing loss. Auditory brainstem response testing records electrical activity along the auditory pathway, giving a threshold estimate without the patient reporting anything. It resolves discrepancies between claimed and demonstrated hearing.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 118

src.question: A 24-year-old reports total deafness in one ear following a minor workplace incident, but startles to a loud unexpected sound on that side and gives inconsistent audiometry. The clinician needs an objective test that does not depend on the patient's cooperation. Which investigation is most appropriate?
src.key: Auditory brainstem response testing
src.explanation: Brainstem response recording measures the electrical activity generated along the auditory pathway in response to sound, so it produces a threshold estimate without the patient having to report anything. That makes it the way to resolve a discrepancy between claimed and demonstrated hearing.

items.html: Rebound congestion. Prolonged topical decongestant use worsens congestion: receptors downregulate and vessels dilate more each time the drug wears off, prompting more frequent use. These sprays carry a three-to-five-day limit.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 66

src.question: A 35-year-old man has used a topical decongestant spray daily for six weeks and now has worse congestion than when he started. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Rebound congestion from prolonged topical decongestant use
src.explanation: Topical alpha agonists constrict the nasal vessels, but with sustained use the receptors downregulate and the vessels dilate more each time the drug wears off. The patient then uses it more often, and the congestion worsens. That is why these sprays carry a three-to-five-day limit.

items.html: Pharyngitis, tonsillitis, pharyngotonsillitis. The terms name which structure is inflamed: tonsillitis if the tonsils, pharyngitis if the throat, pharyngotonsillitis if both. They are not different diseases and the same organisms cause all; tonsillar involvement raises the possibility of peritonsillar abscess.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 69

src.question: A 20-year-old has a three-day sore throat with fever. On examination the palatine tonsils are enlarged and exudative and the surrounding pharyngeal wall is also erythematous. The clinician is choosing the correct term for the documentation. How are pharyngitis, tonsillitis and pharyngotonsillitis distinguished?
src.key: Tonsillitis if the tonsils are affected, pharyngitis if the throat is, both if both
src.explanation: The three terms describe which structure is inflamed rather than three different diseases, and the same organisms cause all of them. Naming them separately matters mainly because tonsillar involvement raises the possibility of complications such as peritonsillar abscess.

also.explanation: The three terms describe which structure is inflamed: tonsillitis if the tonsils, pharyngitis if the throat, and pharyngotonsillitis if both. They are not three different diseases, and the same organisms cause all of them, but tonsillar involvement raises the possibility of complications such as peritonsillar abscess.

items.html: Timing of nasal fracture reduction. A displaced fracture is straightened once swelling settles, within about two weeks. Swelling obscures bony position, and the bones begin to unite after roughly two weeks.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 46

src.question: A 26-year-old man with a displaced nasal fracture presents four days after injury with marked swelling. He asks when it can be straightened. What should the patient be told?
src.key: Once the swelling settles, within about two weeks
src.explanation: Marked swelling obscures the underlying bony position, so reduction attempted immediately risks an inaccurate result. Waiting a few days lets the edema settle, but the bones begin to unite after roughly two weeks, so there is a window in which reduction is both accurate and still possible.

items.html: Saddle nose deformity. Septal cartilage has no blood supply of its own and depends on perichondrium. A hematoma strips it away, causing avascular necrosis and collapse of the dorsum, which is why drainage is urgent rather than elective.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 32

src.question: A 25-year-old was struck on the nose three weeks ago and was seen at the time but not examined internally. The patient now has persistent nasal obstruction and has noticed the bridge of the nose has sunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Saddle nose deformity from cartilage necrosis
src.explanation: The septal cartilage has no blood supply of its own and depends entirely on the overlying perichondrium. A hematoma strips the perichondrium away, the cartilage undergoes avascular necrosis, and the dorsum loses its structural support and collapses. That is why drainage is urgent rather than elective.

items.html: Nasal polyps after surgery. Recurrence is expected, because polyps arise from ongoing mucosal inflammation and surgery gives only temporary relief. Medical treatment of the underlying inflammation continues afterwards.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 63

src.question: A 52-year-old man with nasal polyps had endoscopic sinus surgery two years ago and his symptoms have returned. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: Recurrence is expected after surgery
src.explanation: Polyps arise from ongoing mucosal inflammation, and removing them does not remove the process that produced them. Surgery provides only temporary relief, which is why medical treatment of the underlying inflammation continues afterwards and why patients should be told to expect this.

items.html: Watchful waiting in acute otitis media. Observation is reasonable with a plan to treat if not improving, provided the child is older, disease is mild and follow-up is reliable. Start antibiotics if there is no improvement in 48 to 72 hours.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 26

src.question: A 6-year-old with mild acute otitis media, no severe pain and reliable parents is considered for observation rather than immediate antibiotics. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Observation is reasonable with a plan to treat if not improving
src.explanation: Many episodes resolve without antibiotics, and watchful waiting reduces unnecessary prescribing and side effects. It depends on three conditions being met: an older child, mild disease, and reliable follow-up so that antibiotics can be started promptly if there is no improvement in 48 to 72 hours.

items.html: Using an intranasal corticosteroid. Aim the spray laterally toward the turbinate, away from the septum. Repeated delivery to the thin mucosa over the septal cartilage, with chronic vasoconstriction there, is a named cause of septal perforation.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 67

src.question: A 31-year-old woman with allergic rhinitis is prescribed an intranasal corticosteroid. She asks how to use it so that it works and does not damage her nose. What instruction should she be given?
src.key: Aim the spray laterally, away from the septum
src.explanation: Directing the spray at the septum delivers the drug repeatedly to the thin mucosa over the cartilage, and chronic vasoconstriction there is one of the named causes of septal perforation. Aiming laterally toward the turbinate treats the tissue that is actually swollen and keeps the drug off the septum.

items.html: Otitis media failing amoxicillin. Persisting fever and a bulging drum after 72 hours of adequate first-line therapy suggest a beta-lactamase producing organism, typically Haemophilus influenzae or Moraxella catarrhalis. Change to amoxicillin-clavulanate, which keeps pneumococcal coverage.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 26

src.question: A 5-year-old with acute otitis media has completed high-dose amoxicillin but remains febrile with a bulging drum after 72 hours. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Change to amoxicillin-clavulanate
src.explanation: Failure after 72 hours of adequate first-line therapy suggests a beta-lactamase producing organism, typically Haemophilus influenzae or Moraxella catarrhalis, which amoxicillin alone does not cover. Adding clavulanate restores activity against those organisms without abandoning the pneumococcal coverage that amoxicillin provides.

items.html: Otosclerosis on tuning fork testing. Abnormal bone fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, so bone conduction exceeds air conduction on the affected side (reversed Rinne). The cochlea is normal, so this is a conductive loss.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 65

src.question: A 30-year-old man is admitted for stapedectomy to treat otosclerosis. He has had progressive hearing loss in the right ear over several years.
