His mother had the same condition in her forties and had a successful operation. Weber and Rinne testing is performed before surgery. Which finding would be expected on tuning fork testing?
src.key: Bone conduction exceeds air conduction on the affected side
src.explanation: Otosclerosis lays down abnormal bone that fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, so the ossicular chain can no longer drive the cochlear fluid. The cochlea itself is normal, so bone-conducted sound still reaches it perfectly well while air-conducted sound is blocked at the footplate. That is the definition of a conductive loss, and a reversed Rinne is how it is demonstrated.

items.section_title: 1.5 · The tympanic membrane and behind it
items.html: Cholesteatoma complications. Vertigo with a same-sided facial palsy involving the forehead means the cholesteatoma is eroding into the labyrinth and facial nerve canal. Accumulating keratin releases enzymes that erode adjacent bone.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 63

src.question: A 44-year-old woman with a known cholesteatoma develops vertigo and a facial droop involving the forehead on the same side. What does this combination of findings indicate?
src.key: The cholesteatoma is eroding into the labyrinth and facial nerve
src.explanation: A cholesteatoma expands by shedding keratin with nowhere to go, and the accumulating mass releases enzymes that erode surrounding bone. The labyrinth and the facial nerve canal lie immediately adjacent to the middle ear, so erosion produces vertigo and a lower motor neuron facial palsy that involves the forehead.

items.html: Persistent cervical node. A node over 1 centimeter is abnormal, and reactive nodes regress within one to two weeks. Persistence beyond four to six weeks, or continued enlargement, triggers investigation, with biopsy for fungal, granulomatous or neoplastic causes.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 31

src.question: A 6-year-old has a 2 centimeter cervical node that appeared with a cold five weeks ago and has not changed in size. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Investigate further, as it exceeds the size and duration thresholds
src.explanation: A node larger than 1 centimeter is abnormal, and reactive nodes should regress within one to two weeks. Persistence beyond four to six weeks, or continued enlargement, is the stated trigger for investigation, with biopsy looking for fungal, granulomatous or neoplastic causes.

also.key: Investigate further, as it has passed the size and duration thresholds
also.explanation: A node over 1 centimeter is abnormal, and reactive nodes regress within one to two weeks. Persistence beyond four to six weeks or continued enlargement is the stated trigger for investigation, with biopsy looking for fungal, granulomatous or neoplastic causes.

items.html: Wax impaction. Complete occlusion by wax causes a purely mechanical conductive loss; the drum, ossicles and cochlea are normal. Weber lateralizes to the blocked ear and hearing returns to baseline once the wax is removed.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 28

src.question: A 71-year-old man reports gradual reduction in hearing in the right ear over two weeks and a sensation of blockage. He uses cotton buds daily. Otoscopy shows the canal completely filled with firm wax; the drum cannot be seen. There is no pain or discharge. Which pattern of hearing loss would be expected?
src.key: A conductive loss that resolves when the wax is removed
src.explanation: Wax occluding the canal blocks air-conducted sound before it reaches the drum, while the drum, ossicles and cochlea are all normal. That is a purely mechanical conductive loss, so Weber lateralizes to the blocked ear and hearing returns to baseline as soon as the obstruction is cleared.

items.html: Untreated presbycusis. Reduced auditory input contributes to social withdrawal, isolation, depression and accelerated cognitive decline. Framing hearing aids as protection against these is usually what persuades reluctant patients.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 27

src.question: A 79-year-old woman with presbycusis is reluctant to try hearing aids because her hearing loss is not painful and she has managed so far. What should the patient be told?
src.key: Untreated loss brings withdrawal and cognitive decline
src.explanation: The consequences of age-related loss extend beyond the audiogram: reduced auditory input contributes to social isolation, depression and accelerated cognitive decline. Framing amplification as a way of protecting those things, rather than as a device for hearing better, is usually what shifts the conversation.

items.html: Course of acute otitis media. Most episodes resolve spontaneously, which is why watchful waiting is reasonable.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: What is the expected course of most episodes of acute otitis media?
src.key: Spontaneous resolution
src.explanation: which is why watchful waiting is reasonable.

items.html: Necrotizing external otitis. It is confirmed by imaging (computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging) showing infection in the bony structures.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 61

src.question: What confirms necrotizing external otitis?
src.key: Imaging showing infection in the bony structures
src.explanation: Correct — computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging.

items.html: Normal tympanic membrane. The normal drum is pearly gray; loss of that appearance is the first sign something lies behind it.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 8

src.question: What color is a normal tympanic membrane?
src.key: Pearly gray
src.explanation: Loss of that appearance is the first sign something lies behind it.

items.html: Diagnosing acute otitis media. With fever, ear pain and a red bulging drum, no confirmatory test is needed; the diagnosis is clinical.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 16

src.question: A 2-year-old girl has fever and ear pain with a red bulging drum. Her father asks what test will confirm it. What should he be told?
src.key: No test is needed; the diagnosis is clinical

items.html: Non-healing external ear "infection". An external ear problem that fails repeated treatment and now bleeds on touch with an irregular growth needs a biopsy of the lesion, because canal carcinoma is often misdiagnosed as external otitis.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 71

src.question: A 68-year-old man has been treated three times for external ear infection without improvement. The canal now bleeds when touched and contains an irregular growth. What is the appropriate next step?
src.key: Biopsy the lesion
src.explanation: Correct — a canal carcinoma is often misdiagnosed as external otitis.

items.section_title: 1.5 · The tympanic membrane and behind it
items.html: Imaging cholesteatoma. Computed tomography defines the extent of a suspected cholesteatoma and is especially useful when the drum is opaque and extent cannot be judged by looking.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 36

src.question: A 40-year-old man has a suspected cholesteatoma but his drum is opaque and the extent cannot be judged by looking. Which study should be ordered?
src.key: Computed tomography
src.explanation: Correct — it defines extent, and is especially useful when the drum is opaque.

items.html: Unvaccinated child with acute otitis media. Haemophilus influenzae becomes a greater concern, because vaccination is why that organism has become less common.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: A 14-month-old boy has acute otitis media. His parents declined all childhood vaccinations. How does that change the assessment?
src.key: Haemophilus influenzae becomes a greater concern
src.explanation: Vaccination is why that organism has become less common.

items.html: Pneumatic otoscopy. Puffing air against the drum through a bulb assesses whether the drum moves; reduced mobility signals fluid or pressure behind it.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 10

src.question: A 30-year-old woman is examined for ear fullness. The clinician attaches a bulb to the otoscope and puffs air against the drum. What is being assessed?
src.key: Whether the drum moves
src.explanation: Correct — reduced mobility signals fluid or pressure behind it.

items.html: Normal drum. A normal tympanic membrane is pearly gray and mobile.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 8

src.question: A 22-year-old man has a normal ear examination. Which description matches his tympanic membrane?
src.key: Pearly gray and mobile

items.html: Undrained auricular swelling. Left undrained, a swollen ear leads to permanent deformity, known as cauliflower ear.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 42

src.question: A 21-year-old boxer asks what happens if a swollen ear is left undrained. What should he be told?
src.key: Permanent deformity, known as cauliflower ear

items.html: Avulsed auricle. Recovered detached tissue should be reattached; reattachment is often successful.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: A 33-year-old cyclist arrives with part of the auricle avulsed. A bystander has brought the detached tissue. What should be done with it?
src.key: Attempt reattachment
src.explanation: Correct — reattachment of recovered tissue is often successful.

items.html: Auricular hematoma. A tense, boggy swelling of the auricle with loss of the normal ridges should be drained now; early drainage is what prevents permanent deformity.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 41

src.question: A 19-year-old wrestler has a tense, boggy swelling of the upper auricle after a match two hours ago. The normal ridges of the ear are no longer visible. What should be done?
src.key: Drain it now
src.explanation: Early drainage is what prevents permanent deformity.

items.html: Earlobe keloid. After excision the patient must be followed closely for recurrence, which is common.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 70

src.question: A 28-year-old man has had a keloid excised from his earlobe. What should he be told about follow-up?
src.key: He must be followed closely for recurrence
src.explanation: Correct — recurrence is common.

items.section_title: 1.5 · The tympanic membrane and behind it
items.html: Perforation after acute otitis media. A small perforation that follows discharge may close within days, in as little as forty-eight to seventy-two hours.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 47

src.question: A 30-year-old woman has a small perforation that appeared when her acute otitis media discharged three days ago. She asks how long it will take to heal. What should she be told?
src.key: It may close within days
src.explanation: Correct — as little as forty-eight to seventy-two hours in this setting.

items.html: Syphilis testing in hearing loss. When syphilis is suspected as a cause, order fluorescent treponemal antibody and microhemagglutination assays.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 68

src.question: Which tests should be ordered when syphilis is suspected as a cause of hearing loss?
src.key: Fluorescent treponemal antibody and microhemagglutination assays

items.section_title: 2.3 · Tinnitus, and the masses you can see
items.html: Tinnitus. It is sound perceived with no external source, such as ringing, buzzing, humming or hissing.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 44

src.question: What is tinnitus?
src.key: Sound perceived with no external source
src.explanation: Correct — ringing, buzzing, humming or hissing.

items.html: Normal hearing range. Normal hearing is zero to twenty decibels, and the whole scale then runs in twenties.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: Which decibel range defines normal hearing?
src.key: Zero to twenty
src.explanation: Correct — and the whole scale then runs in twenties.

items.html: Hearing screening age. Hearing is screened routinely in primary care from age sixty-five.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 60

src.question: From what age is hearing screened routinely in primary care?
src.key: Sixty-five

items.html: Profound hearing loss. Hearing loss is classified as profound above eighty decibels.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: At what threshold is hearing loss classified as profound?
src.key: Above eighty decibels

items.section_title: 2.3 · Tinnitus, and the masses you can see
items.html: Glomus tumor. Paralysis of the ninth, tenth and eleventh cranial nerves may accompany it.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: Paralysis of which cranial nerves may accompany a glomus tumor?
src.key: The ninth, tenth and eleventh

items.html: Pure tone audiometry. This test presents single tones at set frequencies to find the softest audible level.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 8

src.question: Which audiometric test presents single tones at set frequencies to find the softest audible level?
src.key: Pure tone audiometry

items.html: Syphilis in sensorineural hearing loss. It is specifically sought because it is treatable and mimics another condition exactly; its presentation is often indistinguishable.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 68

src.question: Why is syphilis specifically sought as a cause of sensorineural hearing loss?
src.key: It is treatable and mimics another condition exactly
src.explanation: Correct — its presentation is often indistinguishable.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Tinnitus, and the masses you can see
items.html: Unilateral pulsatile tinnitus. Tinnitus in one ear that beats in time with the pulse needs further investigation, since unilateral and pulsatile tinnitus are both red flags.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 45

src.question: A 47-year-old woman describes ringing in the right ear only, which she can hear beating in time with her pulse. What is the appropriate response?
src.key: Investigate further
src.explanation: Correct — unilateral and pulsatile tinnitus are both red flags.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The inner ear syndromes — sorted by how long the vertigo lasts
items.html: Audiogram in Meniere disease. Loss confined to the low frequencies that improves between attacks suggests Meniere disease: a low-frequency, fluctuating sensorineural loss.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 69

src.question: A 50-year-old woman with episodic vertigo has an audiogram showing loss confined to the low frequencies, which improves between attacks. What does this pattern suggest?
src.key: Meniere disease
src.explanation: Correct — low-frequency, fluctuating sensorineural loss.

items.html: Rinne in sensorineural loss. Air conduction remains greater than bone conduction bilaterally, because a sensorineural loss leaves the normal Rinne relationship intact.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 42

src.question: A 70-year-old man has bilateral gradual hearing loss and says background noise makes it harder to follow conversation. Both drums and canals look normal. What Rinne result is expected?
src.key: Air conduction greater than bone, bilaterally
src.explanation: A sensorineural loss leaves the normal Rinne relationship intact.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Tinnitus, and the masses you can see
items.html: Exostoses. Hard, smooth, symmetric swellings of the canal wall that narrow both canals and trap debris are exostoses, bony growths from repeated cold water exposure.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 48

src.question: A 31-year-old surfer has gradual hearing loss and repeated trapping of debris in both canals. Both canals are narrowed symmetrically by hard, smooth swellings of the canal wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Exostoses
src.explanation: Correct — bony growths from repeated cold water exposure.

items.html: Sudden one-sided hearing loss. It needs same-day assessment because treatment works only if started early.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 79

src.question: A 51-year-old woman with sudden one-sided hearing loss asks why she must be seen the same day. What should she be told?
src.key: Treatment works only if started early

items.html: Sensorineural loss with sexual infection risk. Consider human immunodeficiency virus and syphilis in unexplained sensorineural hearing loss with multiple risk factors, since both can produce it.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 67

src.question: A 36-year-old man with unexplained sensorineural hearing loss has multiple risk factors for sexually transmitted infection. What should be considered?
src.key: Human immunodeficiency virus and syphilis
src.explanation: Correct — both can produce sensorineural loss.

items.html: Neck mass features suggesting malignancy. These are no infectious origin, duration over two weeks, size greater than 1.5 centimeters, firm, non-cystic, non-tender with little or no mobility, age over 40, and tobacco and alcohol use. Size alone is not diagnostic.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 13

src.question: Which size threshold appears on the list of features suggesting malignancy in a neck mass?
src.key: Greater than 1.5 centimeters
src.explanation: The malignancy features are: no infectious origin, duration over two weeks, size over 1.5 centimeters, firm and non-cystic and non-tender with little or no mobility, age over 40, and tobacco and alcohol use. Size alone is not diagnostic, but it is one of the criteria that shifts the prior.

items.html: Jugulodigastric node. This deep cervical node drains the palatine tonsil, so tonsillitis produces a tender node high in the jugular chain just below the angle of the jaw; it is the node examined in a sore throat.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 12

src.question: Which deep cervical node is specifically concerned with drainage of the palatine tonsil?
src.key: The jugulodigastric node
src.explanation: Two deep cervical nodes carry named territories. The jugulodigastric node drains the palatine tonsil, which is why tonsillitis produces a tender node high in the jugular chain just below the angle of the jaw, and why that is the node examined in a sore throat.

items.html: Examining a cervical mass. Also palpate the inguinal, axillary and supraclavicular nodes to distinguish regional disease from generalized lymphadenopathy, which points to a systemic cause such as lymphoma, mononucleosis or HIV. Examine the thyroid, liver and spleen, and auscultate any vascular abnormality.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 15

src.question: Which additional lymph node areas should be palpated when assessing a cervical mass?
src.key: Inguinal, axillary and supraclavicular
src.explanation: Palpating other nodal basins distinguishes localized regional disease from generalized lymphadenopathy, which points toward a systemic cause such as lymphoma, mononucleosis or HIV. The thyroid, liver and spleen are examined for the same reason, and any vascular abnormality is auscultated.

items.html: Neck mass history. Ask about recent travel and possible tuberculosis exposure, along with recent infection, exposure to pets and animals, malignancy risk factors, recent trauma and immunodeficiency.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 14

src.question: A 44-year-old woman with a neck mass is asked a series of history questions. Which exposure is specifically relevant?
src.key: Recent travel and possible tuberculosis exposure
src.explanation: The history should cover recent upper respiratory, sinus, ear or other head and neck infection, exposure to pets and animals, recent travel and tuberculosis exposure, malignancy risk including previous skin lesion excision, smoking, alcohol, radiation and family history, recent trauma, and immunodeficiency.

items.html: Thyroid mass on Hashimoto background. Primary thyroid lymphoma is usually a non-Hodgkin B cell tumor arising on Hashimoto thyroiditis. Aspiration cannot reliably separate a reactive from a monoclonal infiltrate, so proceed to open biopsy, then lymphoma staging.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 45

src.question: A 64-year-old woman with long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis has a rapidly enlarging thyroid mass. Aspiration shows a lymphoid infiltrate that cannot be separated from her thyroiditis. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Proceed to open biopsy
src.explanation: Primary thyroid lymphoma is usually a non-Hodgkin B cell tumor arising on a Hashimoto background, and both fill the gland with lymphocytes. Aspiration cytology cannot reliably distinguish a reactive infiltrate from a monoclonal one, so tissue architecture is needed, followed by lymphoma staging.

items.html: Exposure history for cervical adenopathy. Ask about tuberculosis contact and animal exposure; recent travel makes the tuberculosis and zoonotic causes considerably more relevant.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 14

src.question: A 26-year-old woman returned from a rural stay abroad and now has cervical adenopathy. The clinician reviews her exposure history. What should be asked?
src.key: Ask about tuberculosis contact and animal exposure
src.explanation: The history for a neck mass covers recent upper respiratory or head and neck infection, exposure to pets and other animals, recent travel and tuberculosis exposure, malignancy risk, recent trauma and immunodeficiency. Travel makes the tuberculosis and zoonotic branches considerably more relevant.

items.html: Suppurative lymphadenitis. A hot, tender, fluctuant node with fever after sore throat is most often Staphylococcus aureus or group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus, in the submandibular or jugulodigastric regions. Empirical antibiotics come first, with aspiration or drainage if they fail.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 33

src.question: A 5-year-old has a hot, tender, fluctuant submandibular swelling with fever after a sore throat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Suppurative lymphadenitis
src.explanation: Suppurative adenitis is most often Staphylococcus aureus or group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus, developing in the submandibular or jugulodigastric regions with sore throat, skin lesions and upper respiratory symptoms. Empirical antibiotics come first, with aspiration or drainage if they fail.

items.html: Malignant node features. An immobile, firm, non-tender cervical node raises concern for malignancy: immobility suggests tumor fixation to surrounding structures, firmness suggests solid tissue, and non-tenderness points away from inflammation.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 93

src.question: A clinician documents a cervical node as immobile, firm and non-tender. What do these features indicate?
src.key: Features that raise concern for malignancy
src.explanation: The descriptors that matter are size, shape, mobility, consistency and tenderness. Immobility suggests fixation to surrounding structures by tumor, firmness suggests solid tissue rather than fluid, and non-tenderness points away from inflammation, which hurts.

items.html: After epistaxis is controlled. The patient must avoid blowing the nose.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 51

src.question: What must a patient avoid after epistaxis is controlled?
src.key: Blowing the nose

items.html: Positioning in epistaxis. The patient should sit up and lean forward so blood is not swallowed.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: How should a patient with epistaxis position themselves?
src.key: Sitting up, leaning forward
src.explanation: Correct — so blood is not swallowed.

items.html: Fever in suspected bacterial sinusitis. Before accepting fever as a sign, confirm that the patient is not taking an antipyretic.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: What must be confirmed before accepting fever as a sign of bacterial sinusitis?
src.key: That the patient is not taking an antipyretic

items.html: Viral share of rhinosinusitis. Ninety to ninety-eight percent of acute rhinosinusitis is viral.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 10

src.question: What proportion of acute rhinosinusitis is viral?
src.key: Ninety to ninety-eight percent

items.html: Preventing recurrent epistaxis. A chronic dry nose is a named risk factor, so humidify and keep the nose moist.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 50

src.question: A 79-year-old man has frequent winter nosebleeds and a very dry nose. What advice addresses the underlying risk?
src.key: Humidify and keep the nose moist
src.explanation: Correct — chronic dry nose is a named risk factor.

items.html: Epistaxis on anticoagulants. Prolonged heavy bleeding in an anticoagulated patient calls for a clotting study, crossmatch and count; the clotting study is indicated because of the anticoagulation.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 49

src.question: A 71-year-old woman on apixaban has prolonged heavy epistaxis. Which investigations are appropriate?
src.key: Clotting study, crossmatch and count
src.explanation: Correct — the clotting study is indicated because she is anticoagulated.

items.html: Undrained septal hematoma. The concern is cartilage damage, because the collection separates cartilage from its blood supply.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 41

src.question: A 17-year-old rugby player has an undrained septal hematoma. What is the concern?
src.key: Cartilage damage
src.explanation: Correct — the collection separates cartilage from its blood supply.

items.html: Sinus tenderness. Absence of tenderness on pressing the maxillary and frontal areas argues against bacterial infection: that pain is reproducible on palpation, whereas a common cold's is not.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: A 41-year-old woman with facial pressure has no tenderness when the maxillary and frontal areas are pressed. How does that help?
src.key: It argues against bacterial infection
src.explanation: Correct — that pain is reproducible on palpation; a common cold's is not.

items.html: Nasal foreign body diagnosis. Direct visualization establishes the diagnosis; imaging is rarely needed.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 54

src.question: A 4-year-old boy is suspected of having a bead in his nose. What establishes the diagnosis?
src.key: Direct visualization
src.explanation: Correct — imaging is rarely needed.

items.html: Septal perforation. Management is to treat the cause; otherwise, septoplasty.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 40

src.question: A 40-year-old woman with a septal perforation from prolonged intranasal steroid use asks whether it can heal. What should she be told?
src.key: Treat the cause; else septoplasty

items.html: Early, mild rhinosinusitis. With afebrile course, clear discharge and pressure not reproduced on palpation, use symptomatic treatment alone, since most acute rhinosinusitis is viral and improves without antibiotics.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 22

src.question: A 31-year-old woman has four days of nasal congestion, facial pressure and clear discharge after a cold. She is afebrile and the pressure is not reproduced by pressing over her cheeks. What is the appropriate management?
src.key: Symptomatic treatment alone
src.explanation: Most acute rhinosinusitis is viral and improves without antibiotics.

items.html: Fungus ball. In an immunocompetent patient with unilateral sinus disease and no bony erosion, surgery alone is the treatment. Antifungals are added only if bony erosion has occurred.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 30

src.question: A 52-year-old immunocompetent woman has unilateral sinus disease with a fungus ball on imaging and no bony erosion. How is she treated?
src.key: Surgery alone
src.explanation: Antifungals are added only if bony erosion has occurred.

items.html: Sinusitis with orbital signs. Diplopia and periorbital swelling are named urgent features, so the priority is urgent computed tomography.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 21

src.question: A 36-year-old man being treated for sinusitis returns with double vision and swelling around the right eye. What is the priority?
src.key: Urgent computed tomography
src.explanation: Diplopia and periorbital swelling are named urgent features.

items.html: Suspected epiglottitis. Avoid intraoral examination and venipuncture once it is suspected, because anxiety-provoking examinations may precipitate complete airway obstruction. Mirror or fiberoptic laryngoscopy in a controlled setting is the gold standard.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 63

src.question: Why should intraoral examination be avoided once epiglottitis is suspected?
src.key: It may precipitate complete airway obstruction
src.explanation: Once the diagnosis is suspected from history and general survey, further examinations that increase the child's anxiety, including intraoral examination and venipuncture, should not be performed, because they can complete the obstruction. Mirror or fiberoptic laryngoscopy in a controlled setting is the gold standard.

items.html: Monospot timing. The test can be falsely negative early in the illness, in the first week, because antibodies take time to appear; serology for Epstein-Barr antibodies is then used. A positive result needs no further testing.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 84

src.question: When can the monospot test be falsely negative?
src.key: Early in the illness, in the first week
src.explanation: The heterophile antibody test is very sensitive and specific once antibodies have developed, so a positive result needs no further testing. But antibodies take time to appear, which is why a negative result in the first week does not exclude the diagnosis and serology for Epstein-Barr antibodies is used instead.

items.html: No improvement at 48 hours. Failure to improve after 48 hours of rehydration, antibiotics, warm compresses, massage and sialogogues means an abscess should be presumed. The gland becomes doughy and indurated; ultrasound or computed tomography locates the loculation for drainage or guided aspiration.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 38

src.question: What should be presumed if there is no improvement after 48 hours of conservative treatment?
src.key: An abscess has formed
src.explanation: Failure to improve within 48 hours of rehydration, antibiotics, warm compresses, massage and sialogogues means an abscess should be presumed. The gland becomes indurated with a dough-like consistency, and ultrasound or computed tomography locates the loculation for drainage or guided aspiration.

items.html: Oral cancer risk factors. Risk factors are tobacco chewed and smoked, alcohol, betel nut chewing, poor oral hygiene and immunosuppression. Squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest malignancy of the oral cavity and oropharynx, and prevention rests on tobacco and alcohol cessation.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 145

src.question: A 55-year-old man who chews betel nut and smokes asks about his risk of oral cancer. What should he be told?
src.key: Both are recognized risk factors
src.explanation: The risk factors are tobacco chewed and smoked, alcohol, betel nut chewing, poor oral hygiene and immunosuppression. Squamous cell carcinoma is the commonest malignancy of the oral cavity and oropharynx, and prevention rests on tobacco and alcohol cessation.

items.html: Negative rapid antigen test. In a child with high clinical probability, send a throat culture before deciding about antibiotics; rapid antigen tests are specific but not sufficiently sensitive, so a negative result is confirmed by culture.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 74

src.question: A 10-year-old has a two-day sore throat with a temperature of 101 degrees Fahrenheit, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes. She has no cough. A rapid antigen detection test is negative. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Send a throat culture before deciding about antibiotics
src.explanation: Her Centor score is high, with a point each for absence of cough, exudate, fever and tender anterior nodes, plus one for her age. Rapid antigen tests are specific but not sufficiently sensitive, so a negative result in a child with a high clinical probability is always confirmed by culture rather than accepted.

also.key: Send a throat culture before deciding
also.explanation: Her Centor score is high, with a point each for absent cough, exudate, fever and tender nodes, plus one for her age. Rapid antigen tests are specific but insufficiently sensitive, so a negative result in a child with high clinical probability is always confirmed by culture.

items.html: Rhinosinusitis duration. Acute is under four weeks and chronic is beyond twelve weeks, with subacute occupying the interval between four and twelve.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 12

src.question: A 34-year-old has had nasal congestion, purulent discharge and facial pressure for five weeks. The symptoms began after a cold, improved briefly, and have persisted since. There is no fever today. The clinician is documenting the diagnosis and needs to classify it by duration. How are acute, subacute and chronic rhinosinusitis separated?
src.key: Acute under four weeks, chronic beyond twelve weeks
src.explanation: Acute disease resolves within four weeks, subacute occupies the interval between four and twelve, and chronic is defined by symptoms persisting beyond twelve weeks. The boundaries matter because the mechanism shifts from a single infection to impaired mucociliary clearance with persistent inflammation, and so does the treatment.

items.html: Adult supraglottitis. Admit for observation, intravenous antibiotics and airway monitoring; it progresses more slowly than the pediatric form and often does not require immediate intubation, but intubation or tracheostomy becomes necessary if the airway obstructs.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 66

src.question: A 46-year-old man has severe sore throat, odynophagia and a muffled voice for a day. He is febrile but not drooling and has no stridor. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy shows a swollen epiglottis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Admit for observation, intravenous antibiotics and airway monitoring
src.explanation: Adult supraglottitis progresses more slowly than the pediatric form and often does not require immediate intubation, so observation with humidification, glucocorticoids, intravenous antibiotics and nebulized adrenaline is appropriate. The airway is monitored because intubation or tracheostomy becomes necessary if it obstructs.

items.html: Mastoiditis. The mastoid air cells communicate directly with the middle ear, forming one continuous mucosa-lined space, so infection extends by direct continuity; mastoiditis is the classic suppurative complication of untreated otitis media.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 19

src.question: A 3-year-old treated for acute otitis media returns on day six with worsening ear pain, fever, and redness and tenderness behind the ear. The auricle is pushed forward and out. The parent asks why an ear infection spread to the bone behind the ear rather than to the sinuses. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: The mastoid air cells communicate directly with the middle ear
src.explanation: The mastoid antrum opens into the epitympanum through the aditus, so the mastoid air cells and the middle ear form one continuous mucosa-lined space. Infection therefore extends into the mastoid by direct continuity, which is why mastoiditis is the classic suppurative complication of untreated otitis media.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Weber, Rinne, and reading the two tracings
items.html: Shallow tympanogram peak at normal pressure. It indicates a stiff mechanism, as in ossicular fixation (type As), pointing to otosclerosis or tympanosclerosis.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 25

src.question: A 47-year-old has had gradual hearing loss in both ears over several years, worse in the right. There is no pain, discharge or vertigo. Otoscopy is normal and the canals are clear. Tympanometry shows normal middle ear pressure with an abnormally shallow peak. What does this tympanogram indicate?
src.key: A stiff mechanism, as in ossicular fixation
src.explanation: Peak compliance occurring at normal pressure means the middle ear is ventilating properly, so the eustachian tube is working. A shallow peak means the system does not move much at any pressure, which indicates stiffness rather than fluid. That is the type As pattern and points to ossicular fixation such as otosclerosis, or to tympanosclerosis.

items.html: Unilateral solitary anterior cervical node. Beta-hemolytic streptococcus accounts for about 70 percent, about 20 percent are staphylococcal including MRSA, and 10 percent are viral, atypical mycobacterial or Bartonella.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 92

src.question: A 7-year-old has a unilateral, solitary, tender anterior cervical node following a sore throat. Which organism is most likely responsible?
src.key: Beta-hemolytic streptococcus, which accounts for about 70 percent
src.explanation: Local infections of the ear, nose and throat drain to regional nodes, and about 70 percent of these unilateral solitary anterior cervical nodes relate to beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection. Around 20 percent are staphylococcal including MRSA, and 10 percent are viral, atypical mycobacterial or Bartonella.

also.explanation: Local ear, nose and throat infections drain to regional nodes, and about 70 percent of these unilateral solitary anterior nodes relate to beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection, with 20 percent staphylococcal including MRSA and 10 percent viral, atypical mycobacterial or Bartonella.

Local ear, nose and throat infections drain to regional nodes, and about 70 percent of these unilateral solitary anterior nodes relate to beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection, with 20 percent staphylococcal including MRSA and 10 percent viral, atypical mycobacterial or Bartonella.

items.html: Ototoxicity. Loop diuretics are ototoxic; ototoxicity from the diuretic can explain a sensorineural hearing loss.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 32

src.question: A 67-year-old woman is brought by her husband, who says she never listens to him. She admits she sometimes asks people on her right to repeat themselves. She denies dizziness, headache and visual change. Her only medication is furosemide. Weber lateralizes to the left. On the left, air conduction lasts 15 seconds and bone conduction 10 seconds; on the right, air conduction lasts 22 seconds and bone conduction 10 seconds. What is the most likely cause?
src.key: Ototoxicity from the diuretic
src.explanation: Both ears have air conduction longer than bone conduction, which is the normal Rinne pattern and is also what a sensorineural ear gives, so the loss must be sensorineural rather than conductive. Weber lateralizing to the left means the RIGHT is the worse ear, matching her symptom. Loop diuretics are ototoxic, and that is the only exposure in the history.

items.html: Persistent lymphadenopathy in an immunocompromised host. If bacterial cultures are negative and antibiotics fail, send fungal cultures and serology; fungal causes are most commonly Candida, Histoplasma and Aspergillus.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 35

src.question: A 55-year-old woman on immunosuppression after transplantation has persistent cervical lymphadenopathy. Bacterial cultures are negative and antibiotics have failed. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Send fungal cultures and serology
src.explanation: Immunocompromised patients are particularly susceptible to fungal infection, most commonly Candida, Histoplasma and Aspergillus, and fungal cultures AND serology are required to make the diagnosis. Negative bacterial cultures with antibiotic failure in this host is precisely the setting in which to look.

also.explanation: Immunocompromised patients are particularly susceptible to Candida, Histoplasma and Aspergillus, and both fungal cultures AND serology are required, because they are not found unless specifically sought. Negative bacterial cultures with antibiotic failure in this host is exactly the setting to look.

items.html: Declining epiglottitis. Haemophilus influenzae type B vaccination explains it: the commonest pediatric pathogen, with routine immunization reducing supraglottitis by over 90 percent. It still occurs in unimmunized children.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 60

src.question: A 6-year-old with suspected epiglottitis is transferred to theater. A student asks why the incidence of this disease has fallen so sharply. What is the explanation?
src.key: Haemophilus influenzae type B vaccination
src.explanation: The commonest pathogen in the pediatric population is Haemophilus influenzae type B, and routine immunization has reduced the incidence of supraglottitis by over 90 percent. It still occurs, from Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus and beta-hemolytic streptococci and in unimmunized children, which is why awareness still matters.

items.html: Ludwig angina in diabetes. Klebsiella is more often involved in patients with diabetes, and those patients may have a more aggressive clinical course.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 108

src.question: A 44-year-old man with Ludwig angina and diabetes is noted to have a more aggressive course than expected. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: Klebsiella is more often involved in patients with diabetes
src.explanation: The usual organisms are streptococci, staphylococci, Bacteroides and Fusobacterium, but Klebsiella features specifically in patients with diabetes, and that those patients may have a more aggressive clinical course. That changes both the expected tempo and the antibiotic choice.

items.html: Facial palsy in necrotising otitis externa. It means the infection has reached the skull base and facial nerve, marking advanced disease and a worse prognosis.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 43

src.question: A 74-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has severe left ear pain and discharge that has not responded to topical treatment. She now has a left-sided facial droop involving the forehead. Inflammatory markers are raised. What does this new finding indicate?
src.key: It has reached the skull base and facial nerve
src.explanation: Necrotising otitis externa spreads from the canal into the temporal bone as an osteomyelitis, usually Pseudomonas in a diabetic or immunocompromised host. The facial nerve runs through that bone, so a lower motor neuron palsy involving the forehead signals the infection has reached it, which marks advanced disease and a worse prognosis.

items.html: Infected branchial cleft cyst. Control the infection first, then excise the cyst and its tract; leaving the tract behind is what causes recurrence.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 22

src.question: A 21-year-old man has a tender, fluctuant swelling at the anterior border of the right sternocleidomastoid with overlying erythema, which appeared after an upper respiratory infection. He recalls a small painless lump in the same place for years. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Control the infection first, then excise the cyst and its tract
src.explanation: A branchial cleft cyst arises from pharyngobranchial ducts that failed to obliterate, and it usually declares itself when it becomes infected after an upper respiratory infection. The infection is settled first, then the cyst AND its tract are excised, because leaving the tract behind is what causes recurrence.

items.html: Dental abscess in an unrestorable tooth. Extraction followed by curettage of the apical tissue, because leaving infected granulation tissue behind lets infection persist in the socket.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 117

src.question: A 40-year-old man has a dental abscess. The tooth is badly broken down and cannot be restored. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Extraction followed by curettage of the apical tissue
src.explanation: The management depends on whether the tooth can be saved. If it can be restored, a root canal removes the infected pulp and preserves the tooth. If it cannot, extraction is required, and the apical tissue is curetted because leaving infected granulation tissue behind allows the infection to persist in the socket.

items.html: Retropharyngeal abscess. The space extends to the posterior mediastinum, giving infection a direct route into the chest; mediastinitis carries a 50 percent mortality.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 107

src.question: A 4-year-old has fever, refusal to eat, drooling and neck stiffness four days after a sore throat. The child holds the neck rigidly and a lateral neck radiograph shows widening of the prevertebral soft tissues. The parent asks why this is treated so urgently. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: The space extends to the posterior mediastinum
src.explanation: The retropharyngeal space runs from the base of the skull to the posterior mediastinum, so an abscess there has a direct anatomical route into the chest. Mediastinitis carries a 50 percent mortality, and the danger space beyond it is continuous left to right, which lets infection cross to either side.

also.key: Its space extends to the posterior mediastinum
also.explanation: The retropharyngeal space runs from the base of the skull to the posterior mediastinum, giving infection a direct anatomical route into the chest. Mediastinitis carries 50 percent mortality, and the danger space beyond is continuous left to right.

items.html: Preventing otitis externa. Dry the ears after swimming and avoid cotton buds: retained water raises the pH and macerates the skin, while cotton buds strip the protective wax and abrade the epithelium.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 41

src.question: A 15-year-old competitive swimmer has had three episodes of otitis externa this season and asks how to prevent recurrence. What advice should be given to prevent recurrence?
src.key: Dry the ears after swimming and avoid cotton buds
src.explanation: The canal's defenses are its acidic pH and its intact skin barrier with a wax coating. Retained water raises the pH and macerates the skin, while cotton buds strip the protective wax and abrade the epithelium. Removing both insults addresses the two mechanisms that let Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus overgrow.

items.html: Neonatal neck teratoma. A large firm neck mass with calcifications noted at birth is a teratoma, requiring surgical excision because large ones cause respiratory compromise or dysphagia.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 28

src.question: A newborn has a large firm neck mass noted at delivery. Imaging shows calcifications within it, and the infant has stridor and difficulty feeding. The mass does not transilluminate and has not changed in size since birth. What is the most likely diagnosis, and how is it managed?
src.key: Teratoma, requiring surgical excision
src.explanation: Head and neck teratomas account for about 3.5 percent of all teratomas, originate from pluripotent cells, and are most commonly noted at birth or within the first year. The calcifications reflect the varied tissue types a teratoma contains, and when large enough these masses cause respiratory compromise or dysphagia, which is why excision is needed.

items.html: Conductive loss from middle ear fluid. Weber lateralizes toward the affected ear (here, to the right), and bone conduction exceeds air conduction in that ear.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 19

src.question: A 25-year-old patient has acute otitis media with a serous effusion in the right ear. Audiometry confirms a marked conductive impairment on that side. Weber and Rinne tests are performed. Which set of tuning fork findings would be expected?
src.key: Weber lateralizes to the right; bone conduction exceeds air conduction on the right
src.explanation: Fluid in the middle ear blocks air conduction but leaves the cochlea and the skull's own transmission untouched. Weber therefore lateralizes TOWARD the affected ear, because the blocked ear is not competing with ambient room noise and hears the bone-conducted tone better. In the same ear Rinne reverses: bone now beats air, which never happens in a normal or sensorineural ear.

items.html: Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy in HIV. It is defined by the absence of an identifiable infectious or neoplastic cause, and is treated by treating the HIV with antiretroviral therapy.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 32

src.question: A 36-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV has generalized cervical lymphadenopathy with no identifiable infectious or neoplastic cause after investigation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy, treated by treating the HIV
src.explanation: Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy is defined by the absence of an identifiable infectious or neoplastic cause, and the neck is its commonest site. It reflects the immune activation of untreated infection, which is why the treatment is antiretroviral therapy rather than anything directed at the nodes themselves.

also.key: Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy, treated by treating the HIV
also.explanation: Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy is defined by the absence of an identifiable infectious or neoplastic cause, and the neck is its commonest site. It reflects the immune activation of untreated infection, so the treatment is antiretroviral therapy rather than anything aimed at the nodes.

items.html: Oral lichen planus. It carries a 1 to 4 percent risk of carcinoma (squamous cell), higher if ulcerative, which is why close follow-up is the point of the diagnosis.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 22

src.question: A 54-year-old woman has lacy white lines on both buccal mucosae that cannot be wiped away. She asks whether it is dangerous. What should the patient be told?
src.key: It carries a 1 to 4 percent risk of carcinoma
src.explanation: Oral lichen planus is a chronic autoimmune condition in which activated lymphocytes destroy the basal layer, and between 1 and 4 percent progress to squamous cell carcinoma. The risk is higher with ulcerative lesions, which is why close follow-up rather than simple reassurance is the point of making the diagnosis.

also.key: It carries a 1 to 4 percent risk of carcinoma, higher if ulcerative
also.explanation: Oral lichen planus is a chronic autoimmune condition in which activated lymphocytes destroy the basal layer, and 1 to 4 percent progress to squamous cell carcinoma, with higher risk in ulcerative forms. Close follow-up is the point of the diagnosis, alongside pain relief and removing reversible contributors.

items.html: Otosclerosis treatment. Stapedectomy and a hearing aid are both reasonable: surgery addresses the mechanism, an aid amplifies. Surgery carries a small chance of a sensorineural loss.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the External and Middle Ear, Slide 65

src.question: A 68-year-old man with a conductive loss from otosclerosis is choosing between stapedectomy and a hearing aid. What should the patient be told?
src.key: Both are reasonable; surgery addresses the mechanism, an aid amplifies
src.explanation: In otosclerosis the cochlea works normally and the problem is purely mechanical, so stapedectomy can restore hearing by bypassing the fixed footplate. A hearing aid achieves a functional result without operative risk, which includes the small chance of a sensorineural loss. The choice depends on how the patient weighs those.

items.html: Chronic rhinosinusitis. Continuous symptoms beyond 12 weeks define it; repeated antibiotic courses treat the flares without changing the underlying problem of impaired mucociliary clearance with persistent inflammation.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses, Slide 25

src.question: A 41-year-old man has had nasal congestion, facial pressure and reduced smell continuously for five months, with intermittent flares. He has had three courses of antibiotics. What is the most likely diagnosis?
src.key: Chronic rhinosinusitis, beyond 12 weeks
src.explanation: The dividing line between acute and chronic disease is twelve weeks of continuous symptoms, and five months is well beyond it. The mechanism shifts from a single infection to impaired mucociliary clearance with persistent inflammation, which is why repeated antibiotic courses treat the flares without changing the underlying problem.

items.html: Rash after an aminopenicillin for sore throat. Infectious mononucleosis, with the aminopenicillin triggering a widespread exanthem; fever, tonsillar pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy fit mononucleosis rather than streptococcus.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 87

src.question: A 19-year-old university student is treated with amoxicillin for a presumed streptococcal sore throat. Three days later she develops a widespread maculopapular rash over the trunk. Her tonsils are enlarged with exudate and she has bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and fatigue. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: She has infectious mononucleosis, and the aminopenicillin triggered the rash
src.explanation: Giving an aminopenicillin to someone with Epstein-Barr virus infection reliably provokes a widespread exanthem, and the sequence described is the classic route to the diagnosis: a sore throat treated as strep, a rash, and then the real cause. The triad of fever, tonsillar pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy fits mononucleosis rather than streptococcus.

also.key: Mononucleosis, with the rash triggered by the aminopenicillin
also.explanation: Giving an aminopenicillin in Epstein-Barr infection reliably provokes a widespread exanthem, and this sequence is the classic route to the diagnosis. The triad of fever, tonsillar pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy fits mononucleosis rather than streptococcus.

items.html: Suspected supraglottitis in a child. Do not examine the throat; secure the airway with the appropriate team. Intraoral examination and venipuncture increase anxiety and may precipitate complete airway obstruction.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 63

src.question: A 4-year-old is brought in with a few hours of high fever, drooling, refusal to swallow and a muffled voice. He is sitting upright and leaning forward with his chin thrust out, and appears distressed and anxious. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Do not examine the throat; secure the airway with the appropriate team
src.explanation: The four Ds and the tripod position describe supraglottitis, and the teaching is explicit that once it is suspected, examinations that increase the child's anxiety, including intraoral examination and venipuncture, may precipitate complete airway obstruction. The priority is a controlled airway in theater with anesthetic and surgical teams present.

also.key: Do not examine the throat; secure the airway with the team
also.explanation: The four Ds and the tripod position describe supraglottitis, and once suspected, examinations that raise the child's anxiety, including intraoral examination and venipuncture, can precipitate complete obstruction. The priority is a controlled airway in theater with anesthetic and surgical teams present.

items.html: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis. Avoid tracheostomy, because it creates another squamociliary junction, a site the papillomas favor, and spreads disease distally into the trachea.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 52

src.question: A 3-year-old with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is deteriorating. A clinician suggests tracheostomy to secure the airway. What should the patient be told?
src.key: Avoid tracheostomy, because it creates another site the papillomas favor
src.explanation: Papillomas have an affinity for squamociliary junctions, the boundaries where ciliated respiratory epithelium meets squamous epithelium. A tracheostomy creates a new such junction, giving the disease a fresh site to seed and spreading it distally into the trachea, which is why it is specifically avoided.

items.html: Recurrent tonsillitis with peritonsillar abscesses. Tonsillectomy is indicated, usually after the acute infection resolves, because the tissue planes are cleaner and bleeding is less.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 101

src.question: A 25-year-old man has had three peritonsillar abscesses and multiple episodes of tonsillitis over two years. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
src.key: Tonsillectomy, usually after the acute infection resolves
src.explanation: Recurrent tonsillitis with recurrent peritonsillar abscesses is the indication for tonsillectomy, and most surgeons prefer to operate once the acute inflammation has settled, because the tissue planes are cleaner and bleeding is less. Quinsy tonsillectomy during infection is reserved for younger children, unresponsive cases or severe airway compromise.

also.explanation: Recurrent tonsillitis with recurrent abscesses is the indication for tonsillectomy, and most surgeons prefer to operate after the acute inflammation has resolved, because the planes are cleaner and bleeding is less. Quinsy tonsillectomy during infection is reserved for particular circumstances.

items.html: High-frequency sensorineural loss. Consonants are high-frequency sounds and carry most of the meaning, whereas vowels are low-frequency and loud; losing high frequencies removes the information while leaving the sound.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 27

src.question: A 74-year-old woman with symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural loss asks why she can hear her grandson's voice but cannot understand his words. What is the most likely explanation?
src.key: Consonants are high-frequency sounds and carry most of the meaning
src.explanation: Vowels are low-frequency and loud, so they remain audible and give the impression that speech is being heard. Consonants sit at high frequencies and are quieter, and they are what distinguish one word from another. Losing the high frequencies therefore removes the information while leaving the sound.

items.html: Auricular hematoma. Drain within seven days; after that, granulation tissue makes drainage much harder.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 41

src.question: Within what period should an auricular hematoma be drained?
src.key: Within seven days
src.explanation: After that, granulation tissue makes drainage much harder.

items.html: Otitis externa frequency. About ten percent of people experience otitis externa in their lifetime.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 54

src.question: What proportion of people experience otitis externa in their lifetime?
src.key: About ten percent

items.html: Forceful exhalation against a pinched nose. With purulent nasal discharge it can force infected material into the middle ear, which risks acute otitis media.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 10

src.question: A 41-year-old woman with ear fullness is told to exhale forcibly against a pinched nose. She also has thick purulent nasal discharge. What is the concern?
src.key: It can force infected material into the middle ear
src.explanation: which risks acute otitis media.

items.html: Diving ear pain with vertigo. Spinning vertigo, ringing, nausea and reduced hearing mean the inner ear has been involved; rupture of the round or oval window adds these features.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 24

src.question: A 25-year-old scuba diver surfaces with ear pain that is now accompanied by spinning vertigo, ringing, nausea and reduced hearing. What does this combination indicate?
src.key: The inner ear has been involved
src.explanation: Correct — rupture of the round or oval window adds these features.

items.html: Fungal external ear infection. Treatment involves clearing the debris and topical antifungals; cleaning matters as much as the drops.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 63

src.question: A 50-year-old man has fungal external ear infection with visible debris throughout the canal. What does his treatment involve?
src.key: Clearing the debris and topical antifungals
src.explanation: Correct — cleaning matters as much as the drops.

items.html: Home care in otitis externa. Keep the ear dry and finish the full course, because the pain settles well before the infection does.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 59

src.question: A 15-year-old swimmer starting treatment for otitis externa asks what he should do at home. What is the correct advice?
src.key: Keep the ear dry and finish the full course
src.explanation: Correct — the pain settles well before the infection does.

items.html: Temporary threshold shift. It is hearing loss recovering in twenty-four to forty-eight hours.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 54

src.question: What is a temporary threshold shift?
src.key: Hearing loss recovering in twenty-four to forty-eight hours
src.explanation: with fullness and a sensation of crickets.

items.html: Weber in unilateral sensorineural loss. It lateralizes to the unaffected ear, away from the bad side.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 42

src.question: In a unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, where does the Weber test lateralize?
src.key: To the unaffected ear
src.explanation: Correct — away from the bad side.

items.html: Age-related hearing loss. The characteristic audiogram is a curve sloping downward at high frequencies.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: Which audiogram shape is characteristic of age-related hearing loss?
src.key: A curve sloping downward at high frequencies

items.html: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss. It demands prompt specialist referral, because the corticosteroid window is short.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 79

src.question: What does sudden sensorineural hearing loss demand?
src.key: Prompt specialist referral
src.explanation: Correct — the corticosteroid window is short.

also.explanation: Correct — the corticosteroid window is short.

items.section_title: 2.5 · The inner ear syndromes — sorted by how long the vertigo lasts
items.html: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Most cases are thought to be caused by debris in the posterior semicircular canal.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 92

src.question: Which mechanism is thought to cause most benign paroxysmal positional vertigo?
src.key: Debris in the posterior semicircular canal

items.html: Sudden hearing loss and vertigo after a dive. With a popping sensation at onset, management is symptomatic treatment and specialist referral.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 64

src.question: A 40-year-old diver has sudden hearing loss and vertigo after a dive, with a popping sensation at onset. What is appropriate management?
src.key: Symptomatic treatment and specialist referral
