items.html: Tinnitus drug treatment. No drug has proved better than placebo; masking and biofeedback may help instead.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 46

src.question: A 55-year-old man with longstanding bilateral tinnitus asks what medication will cure it. What should he be told?
src.key: No drug has proved better than placebo
src.explanation: Correct — masking and biofeedback may help instead.

items.html: Vertigo with crossed sensory findings. Acute vertigo with facial weakness, crossed loss of pain sensation and a drooping eyelid requires emergency evaluation for stroke, since crossed sensory findings mean a brainstem problem.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 77

src.question: A 76-year-old man has acute vertigo with facial weakness, loss of pain sensation on one side of his face and the opposite side of his body, and a drooping eyelid. What does this require?
src.key: Emergency evaluation for stroke
src.explanation: Correct — crossed sensory findings mean a brainstem problem.

items.html: Sudden hearing loss and vertigo after heavy lifting. With a pop at onset, the likely mechanism is an abnormal opening at the round or oval window.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear 2026 - Dr. Jaquith.pptx, Slide 63

src.question: A 35-year-old man develops sudden hearing loss and vertigo immediately after lifting a heavy weight, hearing a pop at the moment of onset. What is the likely mechanism?
src.key: An abnormal opening at the round or oval window

items.html: Laboratory workup of a persistent neck mass. It includes full blood count, HIV and Epstein-Barr serology, inflammatory markers and thyroid panels; the panel is broad because the differential is broad.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 19

src.question: Which laboratory tests are listed in the workup of a persistent neck mass?
src.key: Full blood count, HIV and Epstein-Barr serology, inflammatory markers and thyroid panels
src.explanation: The panel is broad because the differential is broad: blood count and metabolic profile, HIV and Epstein-Barr and cytomegalovirus serology, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, an autoimmune panel, thyroid and parathyroid hormones, and tuberculin skin testing with cat scratch and toxoplasmosis titres.

items.html: Thyroglossal duct cyst. Vertical movement with swallowing or tongue protrusion is pathognomonic: a persistent tract tethers the cyst to the hyoid, so protruding the tongue pulls the cyst upward.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 23

src.question: Which sign is pathognomonic for a thyroglossal duct cyst?
src.key: Vertical movement with swallowing or tongue protrusion
src.explanation: The thyroid descends from the foramen cecum at the tongue base through the hyoid during development, so a persistent tract tethers the cyst to the hyoid. Protruding the tongue pulls the hyoid and therefore the cyst upward, which no other neck mass does.

items.html: Positron emission tomography. It measures metabolic uptake of tagged glucose, higher in cancer and inflammation, so a positive result cannot by itself establish cancer.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 19

src.question: What does a positron emission tomography scan measure?
src.key: Metabolic uptake of tagged glucose, higher in cancer and inflammation
src.explanation: Radiolabelled glucose accumulates where metabolism is high, which includes malignancy but also inflammation and infection. That dual sensitivity is why it is useful for staging and for finding an occult primary, and why a positive result cannot by itself establish cancer.

items.html: Neck mass persisting after antibiotics. Failure of an antibiotic trial is the point to refer to a specialist now rather than prescribe another course, because early and aggressive treatment is needed in some neoplastic conditions.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 19

src.question: A 59-year-old woman's neck mass has persisted after a course of antibiotics. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Refer to a specialist now
src.explanation: A trial of antibiotics is common practice, and failure of that trial is exactly the point at which referral should happen rather than another course being prescribed. Early and aggressive treatment is needed in some neoplastic conditions, so the delay costs more than the referral.

items.html: Infantile hemangioma. Observation is the default because about 90 percent involute, but airway compromise, skin ulceration, dysphagia, thrombocytopenia or cardiac failure call for intervention; start propranolol, first line for infants without a contraindication.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 27

src.question: A 4-month-old has a large neck hemangioma and is now developing stridor and difficulty feeding. What is the most appropriate management?
src.key: Start propranolol
src.explanation: Observation is the default because about 90 percent involute, but intervention is indicated for airway compromise, skin ulceration, dysphagia, thrombocytopenia or cardiac failure. Stridor and feeding difficulty are two of those, and propranolol is first line for infants without a contraindication.

items.html: Infected congenital neck cyst. Control the infection first, then excise the cyst and its tract; the tract must be removed too, because leaving it behind causes recurrence.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 22

src.question: A 20-year-old man has a tender fluctuant swelling at the anterior border of the right sternocleidomastoid with overlying redness, appearing after a cold. He recalls a small painless lump there for years. What is the most appropriate management?
src.key: Control the infection, then excise the cyst and its tract
src.explanation: The cyst is congenital and only declares itself when it becomes infected after an upper respiratory infection. Settling the infection first gives cleaner planes, and the definitive operation must take the TRACT as well as the cyst, because leaving the tract behind is what causes recurrence.

items.html: General symptoms of a concerning neck mass. Fever, postnasal drip, rhinorrhea, sore throat, otalgia, night sweats, weight loss, malaise, dysphagia and hoarseness accompany it; hoarseness and dysphagia suggest upper aerodigestive tract involvement.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 15

src.question: A 58-year-old man with a neck mass reports night sweats, weight loss, hoarseness and dysphagia. What do these symptoms indicate?
src.key: These are the general symptoms that accompany a concerning neck mass
src.explanation: The general clinical presentation listed includes fever, postnasal drip, rhinorrhea, sore throat, otalgia, night sweats, weight loss, malaise, dysphagia and hoarseness. Hoarseness and dysphagia in particular suggest involvement of the upper aerodigestive tract.

items.html: Incidental thyroid nodule. Nodules over 1 centimeter found incidentally warrant evaluation: ultrasound with fine needle aspiration plus thyroid-stimulating hormone and thyroid hormones, asking about recent growth, dysphagia or obstruction.
cites: CMS I Neoplasms and Neck Masses, Slide 40

src.question: A 46-year-old man has a 1.4 centimeter thyroid nodule found incidentally on imaging done for another reason. What is the correct approach?
src.key: Nodules over 1 centimeter found incidentally warrant evaluation
src.explanation: Incidental nodules greater than 1 centimeter should be evaluated further, and this one exceeds that. Evaluation means ultrasound with fine needle aspiration plus thyroid-stimulating hormone and thyroid hormones, with recent growth, dysphagia or obstruction as the concerning symptoms to ask about.

items.html: Sinusitis in immunocompromised patients. Fungi are the organisms that cause it.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 12

src.question: Which organisms cause sinusitis in immunocompromised patients?
src.key: Fungi

items.html: Recurrent nosebleeds in children. The commonest cause is trauma from the child's own finger, with a chronic dry nose as a risk factor.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 45

src.question: A 7-year-old boy has recurrent winter nosebleeds. His mother asks why they keep happening. What is the commonest cause?
src.key: Trauma from his own finger
src.explanation: with chronic dry nose as a risk factor.

items.html: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and sex. Incidence is two to threefold higher in males.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 69

src.question: A 54-year-old man is diagnosed with nasopharyngeal carcinoma. How does incidence differ between the sexes?
src.key: Two to threefold higher in males

items.html: Nasal discharge color. Yellow or green is the least helpful color for deciding on antibiotics; color barely helps, and only black, rust or pure clear carry any signal.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: A 47-year-old woman asks whether her green nasal discharge proves she needs antibiotics. What should she be told?
src.key: Yellow or green is the least helpful color
src.explanation: Color barely helps; only black, rust or pure clear carry any signal.

items.html: Bacterial sinusitis. Double worsening, unilateral pain reproduced on palpation and fever together point to a bacterial cause; start amoxicillin with clavulanate.
cites: hughie Nose & Paranasal Sinuses fall 2026.pptx, Slide 23

src.question: A 44-year-old man had a cold that improved by day four, then worsened on day seven with right-sided facial pain, purulent discharge and a temperature of 38.5 degrees Celsius. Pressing over the right maxilla reproduces his pain. What should be done?
src.key: Start amoxicillin with clavulanate
src.explanation: Double worsening, unilateral pain reproduced on palpation and fever together point bacterial.

items.html: Minor aphthous ulcers. They are the commonest form, under 1 centimeter, preceded by burning and tingling, painful, and heal in 7 to 10 days without scarring.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 16

src.question: How are minor aphthous ulcers characterized?
src.key: Under 1 centimeter, commonest, healing in 7 to 10 days
src.explanation: Minor aphthae are the commonest form, under a centimeter, preceded by burning and tingling, painful, and healing within 7 to 10 days without scarring. Major ulcers exceed a centimeter, are more painful, may scar and last over a month; herpetiform ulcers are numerous 1 to 3 millimeter lesions that also scar and persist.

items.html: Laryngeal electromyography in vocal cord paralysis. It predicts whether function will return by showing whether the nerve is still in continuity, which decides between waiting and proceeding to medialization or thyroplasty.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 56

src.question: What does laryngeal electromyography contribute in vocal cord paralysis?
src.key: It predicts whether function will return
src.explanation: Electromyography distinguishes a nerve still in continuity from one that is not. A bruised or stretched nerve may recover over 6 months to a year, whereas a transected nerve or one infiltrated by malignancy will not, and that determines whether to wait or proceed to medialisation or thyroplasty.

items.html: Oral lichen planus. 1 to 4 percent progress to squamous cell carcinoma, higher with ulcerative lesions, so close follow-up is the point of making the diagnosis.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 22

src.question: What proportion of oral lichen planus progresses to squamous cell carcinoma?
src.key: 1 to 4 percent, higher with ulcerative lesions
src.explanation: The malignant potential is modest but real, and it is higher in ulcerative forms. That is the reason close follow-up is the point of making the diagnosis, alongside pain relief and removing reversible contributors such as medications, dental restorations, tobacco and alcohol.

items.html: Mucous membrane involvement in systemic lupus. About 40 percent of patients have it, and oral lesions may be the first sign; the oral ulcers do not correlate with systemic activity.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 23

src.question: What proportion of patients with systemic lupus have mucous membrane involvement?
src.key: About 40 percent
src.explanation: Around 40 percent of lupus patients have mucous membrane involvement, and oral lesions may be the FIRST sign of the disease. There is no correlation between the oral ulcers and systemic activity, so they cannot be used to judge control.

items.html: Oral ulcers in Behcet syndrome. They are the commonest feature, affecting up to 100 percent of patients, with genital ulcers in about 75 percent that look identical to oral aphthae.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 19

src.question: What proportion of patients with Behcet syndrome have oral ulcers?
src.key: Up to 100 percent
src.explanation: Oral ulcers are the commonest feature of Behcet, affecting up to 100 percent of patients, with genital ulcers in about 75 percent that look identical to oral aphthae. Diagnosis is clinical: recurrent aphthous ulceration in the context of the characteristic systemic manifestations.

items.html: Cause of pharyngitis. About 70 percent is viral; the remaining 30 percent is bacterial, chiefly group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 70

src.question: What proportion of pharyngitis is viral?
src.key: About 70 percent
src.explanation: Roughly 70 percent of pharyngitis is viral, caused by adenovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex, HIV, influenza, parainfluenza, rhinovirus, coronavirus, echovirus, enteroviruses and coxsackievirus. The remaining 30 percent is bacterial, chiefly group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus.

items.html: Sialolithiasis. It causes recurrent swelling and pain that worsens with eating, because eating stimulates salivary flow and the obstructing stone traps saliva behind it.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 42

src.question: What is the characteristic symptom pattern of sialolithiasis?
src.key: Recurrent swelling and pain that worsens with eating
src.explanation: Eating stimulates salivary flow, and an obstructing stone traps that saliva behind it, distending the gland until pressure equalizes. That is salivary colic, and it is why the history alone often makes the diagnosis before any imaging.

items.html: Oral or oropharyngeal malignancy. Suspect possible oral or oropharyngeal malignancy when ill-fitting dentures accompany non-healing ulcers, bleeding, pain, vague discomfort or a foreign body sensation in the throat.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 146

src.question: A 66-year-old woman with dentures complains they no longer fit, and she has vague discomfort in the mouth and a foreign body sensation in the throat. What should be suspected?
src.key: Possible oral or oropharyngeal malignancy
src.explanation: Ill-fitting dentures are on the list of presenting features alongside non-healing ulcers, bleeding, pain, vague discomfort and a foreign body sensation in the throat. Advanced disease adds dysarthria, dysphagia, a neck mass and referred otalgia, so an apparently minor complaint deserves a proper look.

items.html: Periodontal disease. It raises the risk of endocarditis and other systemic disease, including pneumonia and decreased bone density, and with caries is a primary cause of tooth loss.
cites: CMS I Disorders of the Oral Cavity, Salivary Glands, Slide 119

src.question: A 60-year-old man with untreated periodontal disease asks whether it affects anything beyond his mouth. What should he be told?
src.key: It raises the risk of endocarditis and other systemic disease
src.explanation: Periodontal disease is linked to heart disease and stroke through endocarditis risk, to respiratory disease through pneumonia, to osteoporosis through decreased bone density, and in men to kidney, pancreatic and blood cancers. It is also, with caries, a primary cause of tooth loss.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Tinnitus, and the masses you can see
items.html: Tinnitus red flag. Pulsatile unilateral tinnitus requires investigation for a vascular cause. Tinnitus that is unilateral or synchronous with the pulse suggests turbulent blood flow or a vascular middle ear lesion such as a glomus tumor.
cites: 16. Disorders of Inner Ear, Slide 40

src.question: A 49-year-old woman describes a whooshing sound in her right ear that keeps time with her pulse. It has been present for two months and is louder when she lies down. Her hearing is subjectively normal. How should this symptom be characterized?
src.key: Pulsatile unilateral tinnitus, which requires investigation for a vascular cause
src.explanation: Most tinnitus is a non-pulsatile bilateral ringing that accompanies sensorineural loss and needs no imaging. Tinnitus that is unilateral or synchronous with the pulse is the red flag combination, because it suggests turbulent blood flow or a vascular middle ear lesion such as a glomus tumor, and those need to be found.

items.html: Auricle blow that looks bruised but not swollen. Arrange re-examination in twelve to twenty-four hours, because the collection can appear hours after the injury.
cites: Disorders External and Middle Ear 9-2026.pptx, Slide 40

src.question: A 20-year-old rugby player took a blow to the ear this afternoon. The auricle looks bruised but not swollen and the landmarks are preserved. What should be arranged?
src.key: Re-examination in twelve to twenty-four hours
src.explanation: Correct — the collection can appear hours after the injury.
